The First Volume of *The Patriarchal Vehicle of the Foremost Enlightened Ones* Edited by the Elder Yufeng of Mount Jing,
Yuanxin Verified by Wudizhuzhu Compiled by Guo Ningzhi
In the assembly of the Great Being Vimalakīrti, thirty-two bodhisattvas each expounded the gate of the non-dual Dharma. Mañjuśrī said: "Regarding all dharmas, I have no speech and no discourse;
there is no indication and no cognition. It is free from all questioning and answering—this is the bodhisattva’s entry [into the non-dual Dharma]."
The Gate of Non-dual Dharma. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī again asked Vimalakīrti, "Virtuous one, you should speak:

what is the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-dual dharma? Vimalakīrti remained silent. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying, "To the point where there is not even a word or a letter—this is the bodhisattva’s true entry into the gate of non-dual dharma.
(Xuedou cites this, up to the point: "Virtuous one, you should speak: what is the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-dual dharma?")

[The Master] entered the gate. Vimalakīrti did not raise [his voice] and remained silent. [The Master] then said, "What did Vimalakīrti say? He added, "He has been thoroughly exposed. He further composed a verse: "Ha! This old Vimalakīrti, Born of sorrow, falls into empty vexation. Lying ill in Vaiśālī, His entire body is utterly withered.

When the Seventh Patriarch, the Master, arrived, The single room was frequently swept. He inquired about the Gate of Non-duality; At that moment, [Vimalakīrti] collapsed right there. If he had not collapsed, A golden-maned lion would have nowhere to be found. Yuanwu Keqin said:

"Nowadays, Zen practitioners immediately claim that remaining silent is 'collapsing. Do not mistakenly fixate on the zero point of the scale! Baizhang Yuanwen’s verse says: "One, two, a hundred, ten thousand, millions— Counting on my fingers, I cannot even calculate the number. For a moment, place it before the dark window; Tomorrow, I shall give [you the answer]."
[This is] Your Majesty’s weighty calculation).
Regarding the Great Being Shanhui of Shuanglin in the Liang Dynasty, Fu Xi, the Great Being Shanhui:
he was a native of Yiwu County in Wuzhou. During the fourth year of the Jianwu era of Emperor Ming of the Qi dynasty, the *ding* [year]...
Year of the Ox. On the eighth day of the fifth month, he descended into the home of Fu Xuanci in Shuanglin Township.
His original name was Xi. At the age of sixteen, he took as his wife a woman of the Liu clan named Miaoguang. They fathered two sons, Pujian and Pucheng.

In the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, at the age of twenty-four, while fishing in Jiting Port with his fellow villagers, he caught some fish; having finished catching them, he submerged his basket in the water and made this vow: "Go!"

Those who were passing through left, while those who stayed behind were called foolish by some people. At that time, there was an Indian monk named Sengtoutuo (Śaṃthoka) who led him to the water’s edge to observe his reflection.
There he saw a halo of light and a jeweled canopy, with a magnificent retinue of Dharma followers. He laughed heartily and attained awakening.

He then proceeded to the summit of Mount Song, where he built a hermitage between two *tao* trees and styled himself the Great Being Shanhui of the Double Forest (*Śālavatī*). There he planted fruits and vegetables.
He worked as a hired laborer; by day he labored, and by night he returned home to expound the Buddha-dharma to his wife.

After seven years of ascetic practice, the Great Being (Mahāsattva), wishing to guide all classes of beings, instructed a disciple to carry a letter to the imperial palace, wherein he addressed Emperor Wu as the "Sovereign of the Nation and Savior Bodhisattva.
The Emperor had previously ordered the gates to be locked in order to observe his intentions. The Great Being drew a wooden mallet from his sleeve and struck it once; all the gates [opened].
He entered directly and saw the Emperor in the Shanyan Hall. He sat facing the Emperor on the imperial couch. The Emperor asked, "Whom do you serve as a teacher?
He replied, "I follow one who has nowhere from which to come; I have no teacher to serve. I serve that which serves nothing.

The Great Being arrived in the capital three times, saving both monastics and laypeople beyond all counting. The Emperor summoned him to the Shouguang Hall, where they discussed the ultimate truth together. The Great...
The scholar said, "It ceases but is not extinguished. The Emperor requested that the Great Being lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
As soon as the Great Being ascended the seat, he struck the lectern once with his ruler and immediately descended. The Emperor was astonished. The Holy Master asked, "Your Majesty, do you understand?

The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. The Holy Master said, "The Great Being has finished lecturing on the sutra. On another day, during a lecture on the sutra, the Emperor arrived; the entire assembly rose.

The Great Being sat upright and motionless. The assembly reported, "Your Majesty has arrived here; why do you not rise? The Great Being replied, "If the ground of the Dharma were to move, all things would be unsettled.
One day, the Great Being appeared for an audience wearing his patched robe, a crown on his head, and sandals. The Emperor asked:
"Is this the Sangha? The Great Being pointed to his crown. "Is this the Way? The Great Being pointed to his sandals. "Is this the secular world? The Great Being pointed to his patched robe.
He entered nirvana in the first year of the Dajian era of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty at the age of seventy-three.
He once composed the *Inscription on the Mind-King* (*Xinwang Ming*), which says: "Behold the Mind-King, empty and sovereign, profound and subtle, difficult to fathom; formless and without marks."
Possessing great supernatural power, he can extinguish a thousand calamities and accomplish ten thousand virtues. Although his essential nature is empty, he is able to bestow the Dharma rules.

When observed, he has no form; when called upon, he has a voice. Acting as a great general of the Dharma, he transmits the sutras through the precepts of the mind. He is like the taste of salt in water.
The blue pigment within the lacquer is certainly present, yet its form is not seen; the sovereign mind is likewise so. It dwells within the body, entering and exiting through the gateway of the face.
Responding to objects according to circumstances, it acts with unimpeded sovereignty; all that it undertakes is accomplished. Thus one realizes the fundamental consciousness-mind.
With the conscious mind one perceives the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha, and this Buddha is the mind. In every thought-moment, the Buddha-mind is present; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha.

If you wish to achieve success quickly, restrain yourself with the mind of precepts. Purify the precepts, purify the mind; the mind itself is the Buddha. Apart from this sovereign mind, there is nothing else.

There is no other Buddha apart from this. If you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing. Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real.

By entering this Dharma-gate, one attains Buddhahood while sitting upright. Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. This is for the true seeker of the Way who yearns for the Path.
Observe your own mind; know that the Buddha is within, not to be sought outside. Mind is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself the mind.

When the mind clearly recognizes the Buddha, one thoroughly understands the mind. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind. That which is neither Buddha nor mind is unfathomable.

Lacking any capacity for true realization, they cling to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence; thus they drift and sink within this state. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace of mind herein.
The Great Beings who have clarified their minds awaken to this profound resonance; the nature of body and mind is wondrous, and its function undergoes no alteration. Therefore, the wise one—
Be at ease and free; do not speak of a "mind-king. It is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, yet it can cause the physical body to act either erroneously or correctly.

It is neither existent nor non-existent, its appearance and concealment being indeterminate. The nature of the mind transcends emptiness, capable of manifesting as both ordinary and sagely. Therefore, I exhort you.
Be diligent in guarding yourself at every moment; even a single instant of unwholesome action will cause you to drift and sink once more. The pure mind-intelligence is like refined gold;

the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind. This treasure of unconditioned reality (asaṃskṛta-dharma) is neither shallow nor deep—this is the state of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Having realized this original mind, for those who encounter it through the conditions of affinity, it exists neither in the past, future, nor present. A verse says: "Night after night one sleeps embracing the Buddha;
Morning after morning one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, he is always in attendance; In speech or silence, we dwell together. Not even a hair’s breadth separates us."

Like a shadow following a form—if you wish to know where the Buddha has gone, it is simply this sound of speech. (Baoning Yong said: "The assembly, this verse by Master Fu Dashi has not fallen into oblivion since antiquity; everyone knows it.

While there are many who have a sudden flash of realization upon hearing it, there are no few who misunderstand it. Xuansha said: 'Big or small, Master Fu Dashi recognized only that which is bright and lucid. Dongshan Cong said: 'Tell me, do monks ever sleep during the day?

These two turns of phrase—'Who says there are no immortals in the world? One must believe there is another heaven within the flask. Baoning also has a verse: 'When one wishes to sleep, one sleeps; when one wishes to rise...')"

At that moment he immediately rose. Washing his face, his skin glowed; sipping tea, his mouth was moistened. Amidst the red dust of the great ocean, waves arise upon level ground. Hehe! Ahehe! Lari! Lari! He also said: Empty-handed, grasping a hoe; walking, riding a water buffalo.
A person passes over the bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. (Duanqiaolun’s verse says: When the dog runs, it shakes its mouth; when the monkey worries, it scratches its head.

Outside the gate of Ruiyan, the water has flowed westward since antiquity. (Zhang Wujin saw Heshang Huairang wearing a coarse cloth loincloth and cited this verse by the Great Being [Bodhisattva]. Huairang said: "This verse attained the Dharma.")

Regarding matters of the immediate vicinity, one cannot compose a verse on that which lies beyond the Dharma-body. Wujin said, "I request the Master to compose a verse. Baohao then responded with this verse: "Last night the rain poured down, Toppling the grape arbor. The administrators were summoned for communal labor; The attendants and workmen were all engaged."

"Supporting, supporting; propping, propping. Propping and propping, supporting and supporting until daybreak—still, how pitiful! He also said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally solitary and vast.
It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not wither along with the four seasons."
The Layman Pang Yun of the Tang Dynasty (who succeeded Mazu Daoyi):
The layman Pang Yun of Nangzhou was a native of Hengyang County in Hengzhou. His courtesy name was Daoxuan. By family tradition, his ancestors had been engaged in the study of Confucianism.
Having attained a slight awakening regarding the toils of worldly existence, he resolved to seek the True Dharma.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he visited Chan Master Shitou Xiqian and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Shitou covered his mouth with his hand, whereupon he experienced a sudden and profound realization.
Later, he became a friend to Danxia. One day, Shitou asked him, "Since you first came to see this old monk, every day..."
"What is the matter with your daily activities? The layman replied, "If one asks about the matters of daily life, there is no place for opening one's mouth.
He then presented a verse: "The matters of daily life are no different; Only I myself find them in harmony. At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting;

In every place there is no discord or strain. Who assigns the titles 'Red' and 'Purple'? Mountains and hills are free from a speck of dust. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions— They consist in carrying water and hauling firewood."
While carrying firewood, he lit it with a stone and asked, "Are you a monastic or a layperson? The layman replied, "I wish to follow what I admire.
Consequently, he did not shave his head or dye his robes. Later, he went to visit Mazu and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?"
Mazu said, "Wait until you can swallow all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, and then I will tell you.

At these words, the layman suddenly realized the profound essence. Master Donglin Gui’s verse says: "The great ocean’s waves and tides are shallow; The small man’s square inch is deep. When the sea dries up, its bottom is finally seen; When a person dies, they do not know their own mind. Master Yunmen Wenyan’s verse says:

"Swallowing the waters of the West River in one gulp— A, B, C, D, G, E, and J. Heh! Heh! Heh! Ra-ra-li! Master Baiyun Shouduan’s verse says: "Swallowing the waters of the West River in one gulp— For ten thousand ages and a thousand years, there is not a single drop."
"One must side with principle, not with kin. It is a pity that Mazu’s mouth was so narrow. [The Master] then remained there, attending upon him for two years.
One day, the Layman asked Mazu, "Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-hu vessel. What is the principle behind this?
Mazu replied, "In this place, there is neither water nor boat; what talk can there be of sinews and bones? The Layman asked Mazu again, "It is not obscure..."
"The original person—please, Master, cast your eyes high. Mazu looked straight down. The layman said, "This single stringless lute—only you can play it with such mastery.
Mazu looked straight up. The layman then paid his respects. Mazu returned to the abbot's quarters;

the layman followed him in and said, "Seeking cleverness, one ends up clumsy. (Miaoxi said: "It is not that Master Ma lacked looking up and looking down; however, he failed to recognize the original person. Although the layman... [text continues])

However, when bowing, one swallows a whole date. Mazu returned to his quarters; the gentleman followed him in and said, "Seeking cleverness, you have created clumsiness; you have saved half. The Layman had a verse that says:
"Having sons, do not marry them off; having daughters, do not give them away. All together in a circle, we speak of the discourse on non-arising. (Jingshan Daowei showed this to Luo Kuairan, saying:)

In the past, Layman Pang had this saying: "If there are sons, do not marry them off; if there are daughters, do not give them away in marriage. Let the whole family sit together in a circle and discuss the talk of non-arising. Later, during the Yuanfeng era, there was a scholar known as Layman Wuwei (Wuwei Jushi). His surname was Yang, his given name was Jie, and his style name was Cigong.

He had studied under former masters and attained genuine realization within the Chan school. He once composed a verse in response to Layman Pang’s, which said: "When a son grows up, he must marry; when a daughter grows up, she must be wed. What leisure time is there to further discuss non-arising?"

Talk. These two worldly fellows took a plot of land belonging to the Sangha of the ten directions and, without registering it with the government authorities, each claimed their own boundaries and demarcations, saying, "I know this. Yet, they constantly proclaimed themselves supreme in places where there is no Buddha.

At that time, there was also one who felt indignant, namely Chan Master Haiyin Xin, who was then residing at Dinghui Monastery in Suzhou. Upon seeing this verse by Wuzu, he too composed a verse, saying: "I have no son to marry off; I have no daughter to wed.

When weary, I simply strike and sleep; Who cares for talk of non-arising? Regarding these three old men who spoke these three verses—whether one keeps one's eyes open or closes them, it is all right; whether one neither opens nor closes them, it is also right. Miaoxi can do nothing but watch from a distance with a cold heart.

Looking at it, it is not non-existent. Ultimately, does the Layman Kuaiyan settle upon the place where the eyes are open? Does he settle upon the place where the eyes are closed? Or does he settle upon the place where they are neither open nor closed?

If he settles upon the place where the eyes are open, he falls into the trap of Master Pang. If he settles upon the place where the eyes are closed, he falls into the trap of Yang Woeiwei. If he settles upon the place where they are neither open nor closed, he falls into the trap of Chan Master Haiyin. Kuaiyan, seeing this—how can you avoid falling into these traps?

He said: "The Samādhi and the Path are not like that at all. If they were not like that at all, you would again fall into the trap of Wondrous Joy (Miaoxi). It is easy to escape the traps of the Three Elders, but it is difficult to escape the trap of Wondrous Joy.

How can one quickly and ultimately escape it? Wait until I have returned to Yanping and settled my daughter’s marriage; then I will come back leisurely to explain it through for you. From then on, his wit and eloquence became swift and sharp, and he was sought after by practitioners everywhere.
Consequently, he went to Mount Yao (Yao Shan). (Master Yao Shan was a Dharma heir of Master Shitou. Yao Shan asked him: "Within the One Vehicle, can this matter still be contained?"
The Layman said, "I merely spend my days seeking a few pints or quarts; I do not know if I can even wear them.
Yaoshan said, "Tell the Layman that he has not yet seen Shitou. The Layman said, "Picking up one and putting down another is not yet being a master hand.
Yaoshan said, "The old monk’s administrative duties are many. The Layman said, "Take care," and then departed. Yaoshan said, "Pick it up!"
"One shot, one hit—that is a true master. The layman said, "What a fine 'One Vehicle' inquiry!
Today it has been lost. Yaoshan said, "Right, right. Because the layman was taking his leave, Yaoshan ordered ten Zen guests to escort him to the gate.
The layman then pointed to the snow in the air and said, "Fine snow, flake by flake, does not fall anywhere else. There was the Chan master Quan.
The guest asked, "Where does it fall? The layman then gave him a slap. Xuequan said, "You must not be so hasty.
The layman said, "If you call yourself a Zen guest like this, the Old Man Yama will not let you go. Xuequan asked, "What about you, Layman?
The layman slapped him again and said, "Seeing with eyes as if blind; speaking with a mouth as if mute. (Master Danxia [Fayan Wenyi], his Dharma heir...)
One day, Danxia came to visit the Layman. Seeing the girl Lingzhao washing vegetables, Danxia asked, "Is the Layman at home?
Lingzhao set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands clasped. Danxia asked again, "Is the Layman at home? Lingzhao picked up the basket and walked away.
Upon returning, she reported this to the Layman. The Layman said, "It is like applying red earth to a cow's udder. This was Danxia.
Subsequently, he entered to see the layman. When the layman saw him coming, he neither rose nor spoke. Yunxia then held up his whisk; the layman held up his mallet.
Yunxia said, "Is it only this? Is there anything else? The layman said, "This time seeing you, Master, is not like before.
Yunxia said, "It does no harm to diminish a person's reputation. The layman said, "Lately, I have been refuting [your views]."
“Wait a moment,” he said. Xiang replied, “If that is so, then you have naturally silenced your own mouth.
The Layman said, “Your silence is your own affair; it has merely made me mute as well. Xiang then cast down his whisk and departed.
The Layman called out, “Master! Master! Xiang paid him no heed. The Layman said, “Not only do you suffer from muteness, but you also suffer from deafness.”—Dana (Danxia).
One day he visited the Layman and said, "Yesterday we met; how is it today?
The Layman replied, "Bring forward yesterday's matter as it was, and I shall make it into a 'patriarchal eye' (zongyan) for you. Xiang said, "As for this patriarchal eye, can it contain Master Pang?"
The layman said, "I am within your eyes. Xuanxia said, "My eyes are narrow; where can you find a place to dwell?
The layman said, "How could these eyes be narrow? How could this body find rest? Xuanxia withdrew. The layman said, "Say one more phrase."
Thus this dialogue reached its conclusion. Xia did not respond. The layman said, "Among all these words, there is one that no one can utter.
One day, the layman stood with his hands folded in front of Danxia and after a short while, he departed. Danxia did not look back.
The layman turned back and sat down. Yunxia turned toward the layman, stood with his hands folded in *añjali*, and after a short while entered the abbot’s quarters.
The layman said, "You went in and I came out; there is still something left. Yunxia replied, "This old fellow goes in and comes out!"
“There seems to be no end in sight. The layman said, “You lack even a modicum of compassion. Yunxia said, “I have led this fellow right to this state.
The layman asked, “By what means did you lead him? Yunxia then picked up the layman’s headcloth and held it up.
[The Master] appeared like an elderly monk. The layman then placed his *fuhou* (head-wrap) upon [the Master’s] *xiatao* (robe collar) and said, "He looks exactly like a young layman.
Xiang responded with three salutations (*yong*). The layman said, "There is still the lingering scent of the past remaining."
Danxia then cast aside his *fu tou* (head-wrap) and said, "It looks very much like a black silk cap (*wu sha jin*). The Layman then responded with three "yes" nods.
Danxia said, "How can you forget your former breaths? The Layman snapped his fingers three times and said, "Moving heaven and moving earth.
One day, when Danxia saw the Layman approaching, he made a gesture of running away. The Layman said, "That was still just casting off the body."
"Posture. What is the posture of wincing? Xiang then sat down. The layman stepped forward and drew a seven-character figure on the ground with his staff.
Xiang wrote a single character beneath it. The layman said, "Because of the seven, I see the one;
having seen the one, I forget the seven. Xiang said, "Give a word here. The layman then wept three times and departed. One day, the layman...
While traveling with Danxia, they saw the river water was clear and azure. The Layman pointed to the water and said, "Even though it is like this, can you still not discern it?
Danxia replied, "Indeed, there is something that cannot be discerned. The Layman scooped up some water with his hand and splashed it over Danxia three times.
Xia said, "Do not do this! Do not do this! He then splashed the layman with water. The layman asked, "At such a time, what can be done? Xia said, "There is nothing outside.
The layman said, "Few are those who gain the advantage; few are those who gain the advantage. Xia had no reply.
The layman said, "Who does not fail to fall into the trap of the advantage? On another day, he visited [the master] at his residence.
The scholar arrived at the gate, and upon meeting the master, asked, "Is the Layman here? The Layman replied, "When hungry, one does not choose the food.
Danxia said, "Is Old Pang here? The Layman cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! and then entered the house. Danxia said:
"O Blue Heaven! O Blue Heaven! he cried, and then returned home. One day, the Layman visited Master Changzi (a dharma heir of Shitou).
As the Master ascended the seat and the assembly had gathered, the Layman stepped forward and said, "Each of you should examine yourselves," and then stood to the right of the meditation platform.
At that time, a monk asked, "Without touching the master of the house, please let the Master answer for me. Changzi asked, "Do you recognize Pang Gong? The monk replied, "No."
"Shi! The layman then grabbed him and said, "Alas! Alas! The monk had no reply. The layman then let him go.
After a short while, the Master asked again, "Did that monk just now receive a blow of the staff? The layman replied, "I will wait until he is willing before it is permitted."
Changzi said, “The layman sees only the sharpness of the chisel’s tip; he does not see the squareness of the chisel’s head.
The layman said, “If you speak in such a manner, it is acceptable for me; however, were outsiders to hear this, it would certainly not be good. Changzi said, “What is so bad about it?
The layman said, “Master, you see only the point of the chisel as sharp; you do not see the edge of the chisel as keen. (Ying’an Hua said: “The wind blows—”)

The grass bends; when the water arrives, the channel forms. Holding it up face-to-face, he cuts through nails and severs iron. Layman Pang opens the inexhaustible treasure trove and brings forth his own family jewels; yet, while he understands his own wealth and nobility, how could he make others wealthy and noble?

Long-beard has long experienced the fray of battle and is accustomed to wearing the hat of a master. In the most perilous and dangerous places, one sees all eight sides clearly manifest. When the assembly of Guizong has settled, if there is even one or half a person among them who is not capable of self-examination, they shall be driven out.
Why? For if a household lacks the *Bai Ze* map, how could such demons and spirits exist? Master Puzhi of Dading (a dharma heir of Shitou) once asked Jujing: [End of excerpt]
The Master said, "These words—few people from ancient times to the present have been able to avoid them with their lips and tongues.
Can you, Elder, avoid them? The Layman responded with an affirmative grunt. Puji brought up the previous conversation again. The Layman said, "Where have you come from?
Puji brought up the previous conversation once more. The Layman said, "Where have you come from? Puji said, "Not only now; in antiquity as well..."
People also have this saying. The layman performed a dance and departed. Puji said, "This madman passes by;
who would he have to instruct in examining himself? One day, Puji visited the layman, and the layman said, "I remember when I was in my mother’s womb."
There is a saying; let me cite it for you, Master. You must not attempt to explain it through intellectual reasoning. Puzhi said, "This is still a matter of past lives.
The Layman said, "I told you earlier that you must not employ intellectual reasoning. Puzhi said, "A phrase that startles people."
"Who can compete with this? One need not fear. The Layman said, "According to your understanding, Master, it may indeed be called startling.
Puzhi said, "To not apply intellectual reasoning is itself to create intellectual reasoning. The Layman said, "This is not merely a matter of one or two lifetimes.
Puzhi said, "As for monks who subsist on rice gruel, let them be subject to whatever scrutiny they deserve. The Layman snapped his fingers three times. One day, Puzhi saw the Layman.
As he approached, Puji closed the door and said, "Old man with too much knowledge, do not let us meet. The layman said, "When you sit alone and speak to yourself, whose fault is it?
Puji then opened the door. The layman grabbed him and said, "Is it the Master who has too much knowledge, or is it I who have too much knowledge?
Puji replied, "Setting aside this 'too much knowledge' for a moment: between closing the door and opening the door, how much difference is there in their rolling up and unfolding?"
The layman said, "Just this one question would have killed you from exhaustion. Pujie remained silent. The layman said, "Seeking cleverness, you have instead brought about clumsiness.
One day, seeing Pujie, the layman picked up a colander in his hand and said, "Master Datong! Master Datong! Pujie did not respond.
The layman said, "The school of Stonehead has reached its end in your presence; it has melted away like ice and crumbled like tiles."
Pujie said, "If Master Pang could not bring it forth, then it is indeed like this. The Layman threw down his colander and said, "How can you know it is not worth a single coin?
Pujie said, "Though it is not worth a single coin, how can you avoid owing him?"
The layman performed a dance and departed. Pujie held up a bamboo sieve and said, "Layman! Layman! The layman turned his head back;
Pujie performed a dance and departed. The layman clapped his hands and said, "Go back! Go back! Master Damei."
When the layman (who was a Dharma heir of Mazu) heard of this, he wished to verify the Master’s realization and went specifically to visit him.
As soon as they met, the layman asked, "I have long admired Damei; I wonder if the plum has ripened yet? Damei replied, "It has ripened.
Where will you apply your teeth? The layman said, "In pieces. Damei reached out his hand and said, "Give me back the pit!"
The layman then departed and visited Fuyong Taiyu (a Dharma heir of Mazu). While Taiyu was serving food, he reached the layman’s place;
as the layman was about to receive it, Taiyu withdrew his hand and said, “Vimalakīrti rebuked those who received offerings with a contrived mind.
Having set aside this single instance, would you still find it acceptable? The layman replied, “At that time, was Subhūti not a master himself? Taiyu said, “That has nothing to do with him.”
[The Master] was about to eat. The Layman said, "When food reaches the edge of the mouth, it is snatched away by another.

Daoyu then set down his chopsticks. The Layman said, "One phrase would have sufficed. (Yuánwù Qín said: "Śāriputra was a master; Fúróng was extraordinary. They were both completely outdone by Páng Jūshì all at once.

Now, as for Páng Jūshì saying 'one phrase would have sufficed,' tell me, which phrase was that? 'Sitting upright, receiving offerings; the donor receives peace and joy. The verse says: Jingmíng rebuked Śāriputra; Fúróng tested Old Páng. Neither could yield to the other; their sharp wits leave no trace to be found. Clouds drift... )

"Rain falls as a gift; thunder rolls and lightning sweeps. Slaying tigers and trapping tigers; emerging from the grass and entering the grass. Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago, yet until this very day he has not attained the wondrous.
He asked again, "Does Master Māda’s point of truly benefiting people pass on to you, my teacher? Yǔ replied, "I have not yet seen him; how could I know his point of being real?
The layman said, "As for this very seeing and knowing, there is nowhere to seek it. Yǔ said, "Layman..."
"A man of the Way cannot speak with only one direction," the layman said. "If you speak with only one direction, Master, you have again missed the fundamental principle.
If you speak with two directions or three directions, would you still be able to open your mouth? Deyu replied, "I truly cannot open my mouth;
this may be called reality. The layman clapped his hands and departed. Later, Master Benchixi (a dharma heir of Mazu), because of the layman's question regarding the cinnabar...
Xia Da asked, "What was the meaning behind the attendant’s action? Benxi replied, "The old fellow is concerned with judging people's strengths and weaknesses.
The layman said, "Since you and I are fellow students of the same teacher, I venture to ask this question.
Benxi said, "If that is so, bring it up from the beginning and let us deliberate together. The layman said, "An old fellow like you should not be telling me who is right or wrong."
Benxi said, "Master Nian is old. The Layman replied, "A transgression, a transgression!
One day, when Benxi saw the Layman approaching, he stared at him for a long time with his eyes. The Layman then took up his staff and drew a circle.
Benxi immediately stepped forward and stamped upon it with his foot. The Layman asked, "What is this? What is this? He then drew [a mark] before the Layman.
There was a single circular mark. The Layman also kicked it away with his foot. Benchu said, "It was there when you came; it is gone now that you leave. The Layman stood holding his staff.
Benchu said, "It was there when you came; it is gone now that you leave. The Layman said, "Fortunately, it is already perfectly complete; your staring at it is merely laborious toil.
Benchu clapped his hands and said, "At such a marvelous moment, one obtains nothing at all. The Layman picked up [his staff].
The monk Zhazi departed, leaving a trail of dots. Benchi said, "Watch the path! Watch the path! The layman replied, "What is it? What is it?
When Master Shilin (a dharma heir of Mazu) saw the layman approaching, he held up his whisk and said, "This does not fall within the scope of Danxia’s mechanism;
try and say a single phrase. The layman snatched away the whisk and instead raised his own fist. Shilin—
Lín said, "This is precisely Dánchá’s pivot. The Layman said, "Do not let it fall into the trap of 'looking' with me.
Shílín said, "Dánchá suffers from muteness; Pánggōng suffers from deafness. The Layman said, "Exactly so. Shílín was speechless. The Layman said, "I told you it was merely coincidental.
On another day, he asked the Layman, "I have a question to ask. Master, do not begrudge me your words."
The layman said, "I request you to bring it forth. Shilin said, "It turns out you are stingy with your words.
The layman said, "This very inquiry has, without my realizing it, fallen into his trap. Shilin then covered his ears. The layman said, "A true master, a true master!"
One day, Shilin personally served tea to the Layman. As soon as the Layman received the tea, Shilin stepped back and asked, "How is it?
The Layman replied, "There is a mouth, but it cannot speak. Shilin said, "It must be like this before one succeeds.
The Layman shook his sleeves and departed, saying, "This is quite groundless. Shilin remarked, "Pang [Ji] has been recognized."
The old man [was there]. The layman turned back. Shilin said, "That too is quite groundless. The layman was speechless.
Shilin said, "You even know how to remain speechless. He then visited Master Qifeng (a dharma heir of Mazu).
Qifeng asked, "Why does a layman enter a monastery so frequently? What are you looking for? The layman looked to his left and right and said, "Who says such a thing? Qifeng—
He then gave a shout. The Layman said, "Right here. Qifeng asked, "Is this the Way of Dangyang? The Layman said, "What about the one behind you?
Qifeng turned his head and said, "Look! Look! The Layman said, "The grass-robber has been utterly defeated. Qifeng was speechless.
One day, as Qifeng and the Layman were walking side by side, the Layman stepped forward one pace and said:
"I am stronger than you, Master; I can take one step. Qifeng said, "There is no such thing as 'back' or 'front. You old man want to be first.
The Layman said, "The bitterest of bitternesses is not yet this one phrase. Qifeng said, "I fear you will not be satisfied, old man.
The Layman said, "If you, old man, cannot bear it, what would you, Qifeng, be able to do? Qifeng said, "If I had a staff in my hand, I would strike you."
He did not cease his efforts. The layman then gave him a slap and said, "Not very good.

Only then did Qifeng begin to take up his staff, whereupon the layman seized him and said, "This thief has met with a total defeat today! Qifeng laughed and said, "It was my clumsiness; it was you who were clever.
The layman then clapped his hands and went out, saying, "An equal match! An equal match! The layman then asked, "From here to Feng..."
“How many *li* is the summit? Qifu said, “Where have you come from? The layman said, “It may be called steep and hard;
one cannot ask about it. Qifu said, “How much is it? The layman said, “One, two, three. Qifu said, “Four, five, six.
The layman said, “Why do you not say seven? Qifu said, “As soon as you say seven, there is already eight. The layman said, “...”
"Stay as you are," said Qifeng. "Feel free to add more," he added. The Layman gave a shout and departed; Qifeng followed him and also shouted.
The Layman said, "Do not speak so brazenly. Qifeng said, "Give me back my master, Pang Gong, at such a moment!
The Layman said, "Why do you try to show off your spirit? Qifeng said, "What a fine greeting! But who asked for it?"

[The Master] called out, “Person! The layman said, “Welcome, welcome. (Ying’an Hua said: To manifest great function through a great stimulus is not merely like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint, nor is it like a swift flame passing the wind. It requires that on level ground there be a precipice, and where there is isolation and steepness, there be flatness. Observe how these two elders entered the tiger’s den and penetrated the source; reaching the point where the patterns form knots and the blade moves with ease, they attained great mastery. Why then have they never reached the mountain peak? As for Qi Feng saying, ‘Return to me the master of this moment, Pang Lao,’ the Layman replied, ‘Why bother with such spirit? Guizong, at this point, intended to fix an eye here so as to cause everyone to have a sudden realization. After a long silence, he said: “Welcome, welcome. "The bamboo shadows sweep the steps, yet the dust does not stir; the moon pierces the bottom of the pond, yet the water leaves no trace. He then went to visit Master Bailin (a Dharma heir of Mazu).
Meeting him on the road, Bailin asked, "Have you ever shared the verse that gave you strength at Mount Heng with anyone?
The Layman replied, "I have shared it. Bailin asked, "To whom did you share it? The Layman pointed to himself with his hand and said, "Pang. Bailin—
[Daowu] said, "Even Miaode (Mañjuśrī) and Śāriputra could not have praised it sufficiently.
The Layman then asked, "Master, who knows the phrase by which you have attained power? Bailin put on his bamboo hat and walked away. The Layman said, "May you have a safe journey.
Bailin did not look back. (Jingshan Gao said: "If it had not been for Master Pang, this point of discourse might well have been misquoted to others. Nevertheless, Bailin lost out to Old Pang.")

[Zhaozhou] said, “Wearing it. Why? At that time, he could not have obtained a broken straw hat to cover his skull; otherwise, what face would he have had to see Master Pang? Chushi Qi said, “Baolin put on the hat and went away. Bring forth clearly the phrase where he gained power.

For what reason did the old man Miaoxi say, ‘What face does Baolin have to see Master Pang? This too is to support the strong and not the weak. If someone were to act as a host for Miaoxi, I would ask them:

‘What is the phrase where he gained power? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! If you hesitate, I shall strike you across the back with my staff! One day, Baolin asked, “Whether you can speak it or cannot speak it, both are equally unavoidable. You—”
"Tell me, what is it that they cannot avoid? The layman winked his eye. Baoling said, "There is nothing more extraordinary than this.
The layman said, "Master, you have wrongly granted this to others. Baoling said, "Who does not do so? Who does not do so?"
The layman took his leave respectfully. One day, Baoling was sitting in the abbot’s quarters when the layman entered.
Baoling seized him and said, “The people of today say this; the ancients said that. What do you have to say about it? The layman gave Baoling a slap. Baoling said, “One cannot help but speak.
The layman said, “Speaking carries its own fault. Baoling said, [“... (implied: “It is precisely because of this that one must speak”).
"Give me a slap! The layman stepped forward and said, "Try giving it a try. Baoling then said, "Zhenzhong (Take your leave).
One day, the layman asked Baoling, "Is this eye capable of saving people from their mouths? Baoling replied:
"How can one avoid it? the layman asked. Baoling said, "Sentiment knows; sentiment knows. Baoling added, "The staff does not strike those who are innocent.
The layman turned around and said, "Strike! Strike! Just as Baoling was about to lift his staff, the layman seized him and said, "Let me see you avoid it!
Baoling was left speechless. Later, he visited Master Songshan (a dharma heir of Mazu) and sat with the layman for tea.
The layman held up a leather bag and said, "Everyone has their share; why is it that you cannot speak?
Songshan said, "Precisely because everyone has their share, one cannot speak. The layman asked, "Brother, why then can you speak?
Songshan said, "One must not remain without words. The layman said, "Truly, truly so! Songshan [nodded].
He then drank the tea. The layman said, "Brother, drink your tea; why do you not bow to your guest?
Songshan asked, "Who? The layman replied, "Pang Gong. Songshan said, "Why bother to bow further?
Later, when Danxia heard this, he remarked, "Had it not been for Songshan, I might have been misled by that old fellow. When the layman heard this, he sent someone to convey his message.
He said to Danxia, "Why do you not realize it at the moment before the bag is even lifted?

One day, while Songshan and the layman were watching a plowing ox, the layman pointed to the ox and said, "It is most peaceful and happy in that state; it is simply that it does not yet know it exists."
Songshan said, "If it were not for Master Pang, who else would have recognized him? The Layman asked, "Master, you say that he did not yet know what there was—what does this mean?
Songshan said, "Before he had seen Shitou, it was not that he could not speak. The Layman asked, "After he saw him, what then?
Songshan clapped his hands three times. One day, the Layman visited Songshan and saw him.
Carrying a staff, [the Layman] asked, "What is that in your hand? Songshan said, "I am an old monk;

Later, he traveled to the capital and visited Chan Master Huilin Chong of Hui-lin Temple. There, upon hearing a monk ask Xuedou, "What is the original source of all Buddhas?

and receiving the reply, "The cold colors of a thousand peaks," he attained realization beneath these words. After more than a year, while serving as an official in the provincial administration of Luoyang, he went to visit Shao-shan.

Chan Master Gaofeng was about to leave his official post to take leave of Shao Shan. Shao Shan instructed him, saying: "With such dedication as you apply yourself to the Way, why should you worry about not attaining enlightenment?
Hereafter, should there arise extraordinary states or immeasurable joy, you must immediately collect and compose yourself.
If you can maintain this composure, you will become a vessel for the Dharma; if you cannot, it will lead to the calamity of losing your mind. Not long after, [Gaofeng encountered such an experience].
He returned once more to the capital and went to visit Zhikai, relying upon the Chan Master Zhengjue Yi to inquire about the causes and conditions [of awakening].
Zhikai said, "An ancient said, 'The ordinary mind is the Way. Throughout your twelve periods of the day, you emit light and shake the earth, yet you do not realize it yourself;

you run outward in pursuit, becoming increasingly estranged and increasingly distant. Gong was even more doubtful and could not resolve his confusion. One night, he entered the inner room, whereupon Zhikai—
The *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) recounts that King Xiangzhi questioned Venerable Prajñātāra, "What is the Buddha?

The Venerable replied, "To see one's own nature is to be the Buddha. When the King asked, "What is the meaning of this? he was unable to respond and was filled with great doubt. Upon returning home, he went to bed and fell into a deep sleep.
At the fifth watch, as he was waking up, while he was reflecting on the matter, he beheld various extraordinary signs; his inner and outer being became transparently clear. Six...

The earth shook and the heavens revolved; it was as if the clouds parted to reveal the moon. Overjoyed beyond measure, he suddenly recalled the words with which Shao Shan had charged him before their parting.
He restrained his emotions for the time being and waited until dawn to relate everything he had attained to Zhihai for verification.
Zhihai said, "You must be able to put this into practice before you have truly attained it. The Master asked, "Is it not necessary to tread the path? Zhihai replied sternly:
Sheng said, "What kind of matter is this? You should rather speak of actual practice. The Duke attained silent realization. (Huanji said:

"The Judicial Commissioner was unable to have a sudden flash of insight amidst the cold colors of the thousand peaks; thus he brought Master Prajñātāra into the ranks of the tailless monkeys, wandering through the cycle of rebirth—how tragic!

He then composed eight verses on "Illuminating the Mind-Ground" and wrote the "Treatise on Illuminating the Way and Admonishing the Confucians" to warn the world. (The text says: "Illuminating the Way lies in seeing one's nature. That which I have realized is seeing one's nature... )

Mencius said: "The mouth’s desire for flavors, the eyes’ for colors, the ears’ for sounds, the nose’s for odors, and the four limbs’ for ease and comfort—these are the nature (*xing*). Yangzi said: "Sight, hearing, speech, appearance, and thought are what the nature possesses.

If one perceives this, one can clearly understand the Way (*dao*). One must know that the Way is not distant from man; man’s relation to the Way is like that of fish to water—they have never been separated from it for even a moment. It is only because they delude themselves and pursue external objects that [they stray]. At last...

The body follows this [Way] without even knowing it. The Buddha calls it "Great Awakening" (Mahābodhi); the Confucian calls it "Foremost Awakening. It is simply the awakening to this. An ancient said: "From antiquity to the present, there has never been a lapse; it is clearly right before one's eyes. He also said:

"The Great Way is merely before one's eyes, yet for all its importance, it is difficult to see while looking at it. Furthermore: "To know the true essence of the Great Way, do not depart from sound, form, speech, and language. And: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him.

Rising and sitting, we are always in each other's company; speaking and remaining silent, we dwell together. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply these very sounds of speech. These words of the Buddha regarding the Way are the most intimate. When standing, one sees Him as if He were present before one; when moving, one sees Him as if leaning upon the crossbar. One looks for Him in front, and suddenly He is behind.

To turn left or right and encounter its source—this is the way the Confucianists speak of the Way, and it is the most proximate approach. Yet why is this? Because this Way can only be transmitted mind-to-mind and does not rely on written words. Thus, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, the wondrous mind was transmitted to Kāśyapa; when Bodhidharma faced a wall, the essential tenet was entrusted to Huike (Shenguang).

Once the six petals had unfolded, a thousand blossoms vied in their splendor; as schools and lineages branched out, each established its own gate and courtyard. Therefore, some signaled with a blink of the eye or a raising of the eyebrows, some brandished fists or pointed fingers, while others administered blows or...

"Ho!"—raising the whisk, striking the mallet, or holding up a staff, drawing a bow, rolling a ball, or dancing with a tablet; or dragging stones, moving earth, beating drums, or blowing the hair-whisk; or remaining silent, speaking a word, sighing, or smiling—even these various skillful means are all intimate acts for the sake of others.

Yet, precisely because they are so intimate, many people are at a loss. Those who perceive them in a single flash are not separated by even a hair’s breadth. Should one hesitate, however, the distance is ten thousand miles. Those who wish to clarify the Way should not neglect this. Thus it has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch until the present day.

It was unceasing. Truly, this is what our Confucian tradition calls "being incensed without venting" and "opening up without opposition. My own attainment has indeed come through this gate. Reflecting upon our Confucianism, it possesses its own path. How excellent were the words of Confucius:

"To silently comprehend and to unify all with one principle"; thus, the Way exists within the very sight of the eyes, and the meaning is understood as clearly as pointing at one's palm. All such matters accord with the subtle purport of the Chan school and capture the true mechanism beyond formal teaching.

Nevertheless, the Way of Confucius was transmitted to Zisi, and Zisi transmitted it to Mencius. After Mencius passed away, the transmission was lost, and what remains in the world is merely the written word. Therefore, my study must seek self-realization before I can rest. Fortunately, one night...

Enlightenment. Whatever is seen by the ordinary eye, heard by the ear, thought by the mind, spoken by the mouth, or moved by the hands and feet—none of these are not wondrous. Having attained this for a long time, it becomes increasingly manifest before me. Whenever I attempt to impart it to others, they are unable to receive it;

only then do I realize its wondrousness. Indeed, the Way cannot be transmitted through written words. Alas! This Way is transmitted when there is a person worthy of it, and it is severed when there is no such person. I have already attained it; who else might resemble me? Thus ends [the text].

Whether such a person as this exists within my own body or does not exist, it is impossible to know. Therefore, I have composed verses, songs, and discourses to disseminate this matter, and have further written this treatise to instruct my disciples.

Zhao Bian, courtesy name Yuedao, was a native of Xian County, Quzhou. His style was Zhifeizi. He served as a State Councilor.

At over forty years of age, he cast aside worldly sounds and colors and fixed his mind upon the religious teachings. Initially, he traveled and studied under Chan Master Fajian of Jiangshan. Slightly...
He had a realization. Furthermore, he went to Zen Master Chūgen of Tenpō-ji in Ōnami to inquire about the essentials of the mind.

The Master said, "You stand at court to deliberate on state affairs, honoring the transformation of society and clarifying the relations between people; how do you have leisure to devote your efforts to this? The official replied, "I have heard the purport of the separate transmission."

"This is something inherent in every person; how could you not be able to do it? I wish for you to investigate and clarify it. The Master then instructed him to contemplate the koan of "The Dog Has No Buddha-nature.
Later, when Huìfú was at Nanzen Temple in Qú, the Master visited him daily. Huìfú never once allowed him to utter a single word.

Afterwards, while serving as the governor of Qīngzhōu, he often sat in meditative retreat amidst his administrative duties. Suddenly, there was a great peal of thunder that shook the earth. At that moment—
He attained realization and composed a verse, saying: Sitting silently in the public hall, leaning back on my empty desk, My mind is clear and unmoving, as still as water.
A single clap of thunder opens the gate at the crown of my head; It awakens that which has been my own from the beginning. I raise my head to the vast azure sky—joy upon joy.
"In every land and within every atom, there is nothing that is not so; yet those of inferior and middling capacity are unable to hear it.
It is merely the wondrous function of spiritual power. Fo-hui heard this and said with a smile, "Zhao Yue-dao has simply struck lucky.

In the early years of the Yuanfeng era, at the age of seventy-two, he retired from office as Grand Master for the Lesser Heir Apparent and settled in Sanqu. There, he associated with mountain monks and country elders without interruption. His name was...
He established a High Studio (*Gāozhāi*) as his residence. To express himself through poetry, he wrote: "Beyond the eaves lies a long stream; beyond the stream, mountains.
Rolling up the curtains, one is amidst the vastness of clouds and waters. If someone asks about this High Studio, how shall I answer? In the clear night, I sleep in peace; by day, I am at leisure.
Furthermore, he composed a verse to reveal his intent: "The golden belt I once wore has now been set aside; The message within this state is simply ordinary. Worldly people..."
"If you wish to know the old man of Gaozhai, he is simply Zhao Sili of Ke Village. He added, "Be careful not to mistake him for someone else.

"Had it not been for your daily admonitions, I would certainly have failed to achieve this result. A short while later, he spoke as usual.

Suddenly, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. He was seventy-seven years old. Fohui praised him with a verse: "In office, he was an auspicious sign for the state; In retirement, he became a model for the world.
The Golden Grain has departed from the human realm; The Jade Tower is now completed in heaven. His sword of wisdom is without the slightest flaw."
The ice-pitcher is utterly pure; the spring breeze flows through the stream-path. A solitary moon shines brightly upon the clouds.
Regarding Minister Zhang Shangying (Sishifa Doushuai Yue) of the Song Dynasty: Minister Zhang Shangying was a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).
His courtesy name was Tianjue, his style name was Wujin, and he was a native of Shu. At the age of nineteen, he responded to [the imperial summons].
He set out for the capital. On the way, he passed by the home of the Xiang family. Xiang had previously dreamed that a divine being informed him, "Tomorrow you shall receive the Excellency.

At dawn, the Excellency arrived; Xiang was struck by this and received him with great courtesy and hospitality. He then said, "As a young scholar (*xiucai*) who has not yet married, you should take my daughter to serve as your attendant.

Later, when he indeed passed the imperial examination, he married her. His first official appointment was as a District Magistrate (*zhubù*). While visiting a Buddhist monastery, he beheld the *brahmā*...
The hall was most magnificent. He then said with indignation, "Is my book of the Sage Confucius not equal to the teachings of the barbarians?
Sitting in his study at night, he leaned over his paper and recited long verses; he did not sleep until midnight. [The monk] said to him, "Sir, it is late at night; why do you not go to sleep?"

The Duke informed him of his previous intention, and was in the midst of composing a "Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha. Xiang immediately replied, "If there is no Buddha, what treatise could there be?

Later, he visited a colleague and saw a scroll of scripture before a Buddha niche; he asked what book it was, and the reply was, "The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra."

While serving as a Judicial Intendant (*tidianxing*), he traveled to Fén to pay homage at the stupa of National Teacher Dàdá. There, he had a dream in which the National Teacher welcomed him; upon waking, he read the records of the Master’s sayings.

The Patriarch called out, “Virtuous One! The National Teacher turned his head. The Patriarch asked, “What is it? The Master then attained realization and composed a verse:
“What is it? What is it? The lamp before the Rāhu Hall— Is it fire? Or is it not? The Patriarch calls out; I turn my head only to be seen through by Sudhana.
The Vairambha wind is fierce; the Nine Heavens are high. The egret’s eyes go blind; the fish dart away.”
In the sixth year of the Yuanyou era, while serving as the Fiscal Commissioner of Jiangxi, he first visited Chan Master Zhaojue of Donglin. Zhaojue interrogated him regarding his insights;

Master Yue was short in stature; the Duke had previously met Gong Dezhuang, who told him that Yue was intelligent and likable. The Duke remarked, "I have heard that you, Master, are skilled in literary composition.
Yue laughed heartily and said, "The Commissioner has lost one of his eyes! [The Duke] followed Master Yue, who was of the Linji lineage.

The Master did not agree with his words, but instead forcefully counted on his fingers and said, "That is the ninth generation. He then asked, "How far is Yuxi from here?"

Regarding students: the first point is that they "pull weeds to investigate the profound," seeking only to realize their nature. Where, then, does this nature reside right now? The Master’s verse says: In the dense shade of summer trees, the cuckoo calls;
