Whether or not this accords with the intent of the Patriarchs, Ciming also frequently cited Fenyang’s "Ten Wisdoms Identical to Reality" when receiving people.

[The Master] said, "I wish to hear your explanation. Juefan said, "The Ten Wisdoms of Identical Reality (*shízhì tóngzhēn*) and the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials (*sānxuán sānyào*) share the same pivot.
Everywhere else, people merely cherish superficial, conventional views and do not believe in the existence of a gate of awakening (*wùmén*). Even if Fenyang were to be reborn..."
Qin analyzed it for him and likewise considered it incorrect. The Duke sighed deeply for a long time and said, "Yet this must be its essential meaning;
could there not be some skillful means [to explain it]? Juefan replied with a verse: "The ten wisdoms share the same reality, their true face complete; Among them, one wisdom is the root source.
If a person wishes to see the Old Man of Fenyang, He must split the Three Mysteries into two sides. The Duke asked again.
Regarding Linji’s fourfold method of guest and host, Juefan replied that the text was too long to be included here. The Master especially delighted in guiding venerable elders;
he once recommended Hao Puchun to take charge of the affairs of Dayang Monastery, and before long, he again requested Hao to reside at Yuyuan.
On the day of the opening of the hall, when all the officials had assembled, Fuhao looked at the great assembly and said, "Do you not see? He said it again:
"Do you not see? Gong Cao, speaking with a Shu accent, replied, "The Master sees. Fuhao responded immediately, "It is enough that the Excellency sees."
He immediately descended from his seat. The Duke then visited the Chan practitioner Ji at Cuoyan in Hongzhou. As Ji came out to welcome him, the Duke asked, "What is the scenery of Cuoyan?
Ji replied, "The gate is near the thousand-fathom well of Hongya; the stone bridge divides the waters as they wind around the pines and cypresses.
The Duke took Ji’s hand and said, "I have long heard of the Chan practitioner's reputation. How could you have been capable of such a response? Ji [bowed].
The Master said, "It was merely a coincidence. The Duke smiled and then recited: "A wild monk welcomes guests descending from the misty peaks; let me ask, what is it that is called 'Cuiyan'?
He then completed the verse with the first two lines he had previously composed. This became a celebrated event transmitted among those in the monastic community.
Previously, while the Duke was at Huilin Monastery, a monk was discussing Chan, yet refused to acknowledge the various schools. The Duke asked him about the response of Xianzi to the Patriarch.
Regarding the "meaning of the West," [Dongshan] asked: "What is the meaning of the wine stand and tray before the deity?

The monk stared straight at him with wide-open eyes and said, "The wine stand and tray before the deity. Dongshan teased him, saying, "If there were lamps in the shrine tonight, it would have been fine;
otherwise, the Buddha-dharma of this 'clam' (xiànzi) has been rendered a mere empty gesture. His entry into the *samādhi* of playful sport was likewise through this skull. Zhenghe.

In the interim, while the Master was in exile at Zhugong, he happened to meet Master Min at Mount Emei’s Middle Peak. Master Min visited him specifically to discuss the teachings of the Buddhist vehicle (*jiao-cheng*).
The Master sighed in profound admiration. Upon hearing that Master Min had become the Head Seat (*zuo-yuan*) of Jia Shan, the Master sent a letter to Chan Master Foguo Qin, saying:

"Master Min, the Preceptor, has abandoned his studies of the Abhidharma (*yi-xue*) and opened the eye of the school; it is as if this ship full of precious jewels has encountered a favorable wind and reached its destination."

[The boat] reached the bank. Daoqin also rejoiced at leaving the gorges. He traveled south, following the current down to Jingmen. At that time, the Master [Fazang] lived as one who had realized the Way and was rarely granted approval by others.
Daoqin moored his boat and went to pay him a visit. They engaged in an intense discussion on the essential points of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, saying:

"The realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the *Avataṃsaka* is the total reality of principle and phenomena; from the beginning, there are no provisional dharmas. Therefore, it is one and yet ten thousand. He understood this thoroughly.
Ten thousand become one; one returns to one; ten thousand return to ten thousand. Vast and boundless, it cannot be exhausted. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Unfolding and rolling up with sovereign ease, they are unimpeded and perfectly interfused. Although this is the ultimate principle, it is ultimately but ripples on a windless lake.
At this point, Master Gong unconsciously drew his seat closer, and Qin then asked: "Reaching this state, how does it differ from the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
"Are they the same or different? Master Gong said, "They are the same. Yunmen Qin said, "At least you have avoided entanglement. Master Gong’s expression turned sullen.
Yunmen Qin said, "Have you not heard Yunmen say: 'Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—there is not even a hair’s breadth of affliction'—this is still a turning phrase?"
"When one directly reaches the point where not even a single color is seen, that is but half-way. One must further know that there is a time for the 'full presentation' (quán-tí) beyond this.
"Were not Deshan and Linji instances of this full presentation? The Master nodded his head in agreement.

The following day, he again raised the matter of the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena, the *dharmadhātu* of principle, and up to the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena. Yuanqin then asked, "Can these be called Chan? The Master—

[Qingyuan] said, "This is precisely when one may speak of Chan. Qinxiao said, "Not so. This is still within the measure of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As long as the measure of the dharma-realm has not been extinguished, it is not yet possible to speak of Chan.

Only when one reaches the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*) and the measure of the dharma-realm is extinguished is it truly appropriate to speak of Chan."
"What is the Buddha? A dried-up dung pellet. "What is the Buddha? Three catties of hemp. Therefore, the verse by Zhenjing says: "In every matter there is no obstruction;
one is as free and sovereign as one wishes. Grasping a pig's head in hand while reciting the pure precepts from the mouth, one drives [the beast] out of the brothel."
"Without yet having repaid the debt for the wine, you have untied the sack at the crossroads. The Master said, "How beautiful is this discourse!

How could it be easily heard? Thereupon, he treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher and invited him to reside at Biryam. Previously, when Chan Master Ledtan Zun had passed away, Dahui had requested a stele inscription from the Master.
Upon meeting, the Master asked, "Why is it that you, Venerable One, are wearing these straw sandals?"
[The monk] arrived from afar. He said, "I have traveled several thousand *li* begging for alms to come and see you, my lord.
The lord asked, "How old are you? He replied, "Twenty-eight. The lord asked, "How old is the water buffalo? He replied, "Two.
The lord said, "Where did you learn such empty talk? He replied, "Today I saw it clearly from you, my lord. The lord laughed and said, "Sit and drink tea. As soon as he was seated—
He asked again, "What brings you here from so far? Mahāmati stepped forward and said, "The Venerable Master has passed away.
During his cremation, his eyeballs, teeth, and prayer beads remained unburnt, and countless śarīras were found.

The elders of the mountain all wish for your Excellency’s masterful pen to compose an inscription for his stupa, to inspire future students; thus we have come specifically from afar. The Master said, "I have one question for you, Venerable One."
"If you can speak [the answer], then you may do it. If you cannot speak it, I shall give you five strings of cash and send you back to Tuṣita to practice Zen.
The monk said, "Please ask me, my lord. The official asked, "I have heard that Old Zhun’s eyesight is unimpaired—is this true?
The monk replied, "It is. The official said, "I am not asking about those eyes. The monk asked, "Which eyes are you asking about? The official said, "I am asking about the Vajra-eye (*vajranetra*)."
Yun-men said, "If this is the Vajra-eye, it is already upon your honor's writing-brush.
The official replied, "I shall provide him with a stroke of light so that it may shine upon heaven and earth. The official asked again, "Your teacher Zhi-quan has known this for a long time.
You have come from afar despite the hardships; have you gained anything from Zhi-quan? Da-hui said, "If there were..."
"If he had attained [realization], he would not have come to see the Grand Chancellor. The Duke said, "Ha! You are a man who plunders empty space. On another day, he said to Dahui:
"I was reading Xuedou’s *Niangu* (Capping Phrases on Ancient Cases) and reached the story of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu, which says:
'In a great furnace of refined gold, there should be no change of color. As I rolled up the scroll, I sighed and said: 'If this is truly so, how could there be a Linji today?'"
Yes. He then composed a verse, saying: "The Master of Horses’ one shout at Daxiong Peak Pierced deep into the skull, leaving it deaf for three days.
When Huangbo heard of it, he was so startled he stuck out his tongue; From this point on, the school’s style was established in Jiangxi.

Later, Chan Master Ping sent a letter requesting the original version of the verse. I composed another verse and sent it to him, saying: "The sticking out of the tongue and the deafness of the ears—the Master has already understood; Beating one's breast, one can do nothing but weep."
"O Azure Heaven! In the assembly at Mount Pan, he performs somersaults; only upon reaching this point does one know the madness of Puhua.

Throughout the various quarters, people often regard me as clever and widely learned, yet few truly know me. Since you, Master, have come from the Dharma-cave of Jiangxi, you must surely be able to distinguish between the superior and the inferior;
please speak for this old man. Dahui said: "The scope of your realization, Layman, accords with that of Zhenjing and Siji."
The True Purity Verse says: Guest emotions turn with every step one takes; Great majestic light cannot manifest. Suddenly, a shout deafens both ears;
Narāyaṇa’s eyes open, and Huangbo’s face appears. Sishan [Dongshan Liangjie] took up this verse, saying: "Yunyan intended to ask Xuedou:
'Since he is refined gold from a great furnace, he should not change color. Why, then, were his ears deaf for three days?'"
"Do you all understand? From the past, no one has recognized his 'sweat-drenched horses'; he simply wishes to re-examine his merit that covers the age.
Gong patted the table and said, "Were it not for your words, how could we have seen the point of application of Zhenjing and Sijian? Had it not been for these two great elders..."
It is difficult to fully manifest the teachings of Xuedou and Master Ma. For now, I shall set forth this verse: "Under Master Ma’s shout, the school’s style was established;
Alas, the three of us share the same insight. The six giant turtles at sea have swallowed the bait; Who else remains to ask the old fisherman as he rests by the reeds?

On the dawn of the fourth month of the eleventh year of the Xuanhua era, the Master dictated his final testament while it was still light. He commanded his disciples to record it in writing. Furthermore—
He composed a verse, saying: "The illusory substance and court robes, eighty-one in all; Like bubbles arising and bubbles perishing, no one recognizes them.
Smash through the void and go back home; The iron ox enters the sea, leaving no trace. Having finished speaking, he suddenly took his pillow and threw it against the door and window.

His voice was like the roll of thunder. When the assembly looked at him, he had already passed away. The Master had a collection of *gū* (ancient cases) and *fǎlùn* (discourses on protecting the Dharma) that circulated in the world.

[When] the Master met Yúnyán, he composed a verse in response to Zhōngdào’s "Ode on Herding an Ox," which said: "Two horns point to heaven; four hooves tread the earth. Having snapped the nose-rope, he herds his own urine and excrement. This was highly praised by many. One day, the Master asked Dàhuì:

"The Buddha possesses correct and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Yet there are still points where he is deficient. Our Confucians even say, 'In the West there is a sage,' and that Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang were all sages. Why does the Buddha not mention them at all? Dàhuì replied: "The Buddha regards even Brahmā and Śakra as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)."

The rest may be understood accordingly. The Duke asked, "How do you know this? Da-hui replied, "My teaching explains it fully: when a Buddha appears in the world, Brahmā leads the way in front and Śakra follows behind. The Duke clapped his hands in approval, considering it a profound discourse. Zhang Wen-ding said to Wang Jing-gong, "Since the time of Confucius and Mencius, have there been no worthy men?

It is only because the Confucian school has become thin and unable to retain its followers that the spiritual essence has concentrated solely upon Mazu and the other patriarchs. The Duke remarked, "These are the words of one who has attained realization. The Duke annotated the *Haiyan jing* (Ocean-Eye Sutra), explaining the eight accomplishments regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard at one time" (*evam mayā śrutam ekasmin samaye*) as follows:

"That which is not not-so is called 'thus' (*evam*); that which is not not-so in principle is called 'so' (*mayā*); being uniquely honored within the three realms is called 'I' (*aham*); and the mind penetrating the ten directions is called 'heard' (*śrutam*). [The text continues: "That which is manifold..."
The essence of the school is called "the One. That which arises from the One is called "time. As Mahāmati said: "Since ancient times, no one has ever spoken in this way.
Li Mīxùn, Minister of the Board of Rites during the Song dynasty (who received the Dharma from Yuánwù Qín), was styled the Layman Pǔxiàn.
In his youth, he read books at the speed of five lines at once; at the age of eighteen, he passed the imperial examinations.
He was selected by his local district for the imperial examinations and soon thereafter rose through the ranks of high office in the capital.

At the age of twenty-eight, he became a Secretariat Drafter (*Zhongshu Sheren*). He frequently entered the quarters of Yuanwu. One day, returning from the morning court session at Tianjin Bridge, his horse leaped;

suddenly he attained realization, and sweat poured from his entire body. He went straight to Tiantong Monastery, where it happened that Yuanwu was coming out of his room. Seeing him from afar, Yuanwu called out, "Layman, congratulations! Great!"
When the business was finished, the Official said in a stern voice, "Monk, why are you letting your eyes deceive you? Wuzhuo then gave a shout; the Official also shouted.

From then on, their exchanges were characterized by such swift and sharp wit that whenever they engaged in dialogue, neither would yield when the moment required it. Later, the Official was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.

He requested a stipend from the imperial court and returned to Lianjiang in Min Province, where he built a hermitage to enjoy himself. One day, suddenly manifesting a slight ailment, he promptly asked for hot water to bathe.
Upon finishing his bath, he sat cross-legged and composed a verse, saying: "In vain have I discoursed on Muxiu and Huhou; today, they are clearly revealed.
The void crushes down Mount Sumeru—what need is there to speak of the path beyond? Having cast aside his brush, he passed away.
Feng Jie (Successor to the Dharma of Yuan of Longmen), Imperial Secretary of the Song Dynasty.
Feng Jie, courtesy name Jichuan, was a native of Suining in Shu. He served as an Imperial Secretary and was styled the Layman Budong (Immovable).

From his youth, he sought instruction from various renowned masters; though he remained on the path of official service, he never forgot his study of Buddhism. Finally, he resided at Longmen, where he followed Fuyan Yuan.
Two years later, while the Chan Master was walking in the Dharma Hall with Yuan, a young attendant happened to pass by the courtyard and recite:

"Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Yuan patted the Master’s back and said, "How wonderful! At that moment, the Master attained realization. In the Ding-si year of the Shaoxing era, he was appointed as a Grand Secretary.
He then met Chan Master Dahui at Mingqing Temple, where Dahui was presiding over the opening of the hall; after Dahui descended from the seat, the Master...
He rebuked him, saying: "Every time you speak to the scholar-officials, Master, you say, 'In this life, I shall certainly not become such a creature.
Why then, today, have you surrendered the pass? Dahui said, "The entire great earth is this Venerable Gaoseng. Where do you see him?
As the official was about to reply, Dahui struck him with his palm. The official said, "I brought this upon myself. (Later, Baifang Shun...)

When the Abbot heard this, he raised his palm in place of the Master [Wuzu] and said, "I consider you a newly appointed elder. He also acted on behalf of Dahui, lifting up his *kāṣāya* and saying, "How many people desire it but cannot attain it?

After a month had passed, he specifically requested alms and sat out the summer retreat at Mount Jing. He named his quarters the "Immovable Pavilion" (Budong Xuan). One day, as Dahui ascended the seat, he cited the story of Yaoshan asking Shitou:
"I have a rough understanding of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. I have heard that in the South..."
"I have not yet clearly understood the teaching that 'directly pointing at the human mind, one sees one's nature and becomes a Buddha. I humbly hope you will compassionately grant me instruction.
Shitou replied, "It is not so, nor is it otherwise; neither 'so' nor 'otherwise'—none of these are acceptable."
"What do you say to this? Yaoshan was at a loss. Shitou said, "Your karmic affinity does not lie here; you should go to Jiangxi to see Master Mazu.
When Yaoshan arrived at Mazu’s place, he asked the same question as before. Mazu said, "At times I instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink;
at times I do not instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink; at times I instruct them to raise—"
"Raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes" refers to this. At other times, he taught that "raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes" was not it.
When Yaoshan attained great enlightenment, Dahui set down his whisk. The Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have now understood the kōan you just cited.
Dahui asked, "How do you understand it? The Master replied, "'Thus' is not permitted; *sulu*."
*Svāhā*. Not so, yet it cannot be otherwise. *Śrī svāhā*. Neither so nor not so—neither can be attained.
*Suru śrī svāhā*. Great Wisdom seals this with a verse, which says: [The] Sanskrit [terms] and the Chinese [translation].
"Crush them into one mass! Alas for the worldly person! To attain this samādhi! Furthermore, Mahāmati recounted this to the nun Miaozong.
Miaozong said, "I once saw Guo Xiang’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi*. Those who truly understand it say: 'It is actually the *Zhuangzi* that is commenting on Guo Xiang.'"
Dahui saw that his words were different from before, so he again raised the story of Yantou’s “Old Woman” to question him.

Miaozong replied with a verse: “A single-leafed skiff floats upon the vast and boundless; Paddling and rowing, it strikes a note apart from the *gong* and *shang*. Clouds, mountains, sea, and moon are all cast aside;
Thus winning the long dream of Zhuang Zhou as a butterfly. Dahui desisted and related this to [Zhao] Gong. Gong doubted what Miaozong had realized.
Not a root. Later, he passed through Wuxi. [Wang] invited him onto his boat and asked, "A woman gave birth to seven sons; six did not meet with those who could appreciate them.
This one alone was not even worth keeping, so she cast him into the water. Master Dahui said, "If a practitioner understands this, how would you understand it?
Miaozong replied, "What has been stated above is entirely in accordance with the facts. The official greatly...
Startled! When the Elder Wulong was conversing with the Master, the Master asked: "In the past, there was an official who asked the Great Sage of Sizhou, 'What is your surname?
The Great Sage replied, 'My surname is He. [The official asked,] 'In which country do you reside? The Great Sage replied, 'I reside in the country of He. What is the meaning of this? Wulong said:
"The Great Sage originally did not have the surname He, nor was he a person from the country of He; rather—"
"It was merely a matter of transforming beings according to conditions. The Master laughed and asked, "Great Sage, what is your surname?
In which country do you dwell? He repeated this back and forth several times. Later, he sent a letter to Dàhuì, requesting that he resolve this kōan.
Dàhuì said, "There are sixty blows of the staff; thirty blows shall strike Dàshèng for not being able to state his surname, and thirty blows shall strike Jìchuān."
When Hehadao asked, "Great Sage, what is your determined lineage? Wulong replied, "Elder, you must go out and find it yourself.
Thus the debate was settled. One day, Dahui passed by Mingyue Hermitage and saw a skull painted on the wall.
He then composed this verse: "The corpse is here; where is the person? Only then do we know that the single spirit does not dwell within the skin-bag."—Dahui.
He refused. He instead composed a verse, saying: "This very physical form is that person; one spiritual soul within a skin-bag;
a skin-bag containing one spiritual soul. Master Gong sighed in admiration. Later, when Master Gong governed Qiong Prefecture, he remained diligent and tireless in his leisure time.
He once sang of himself: "In my spare moments from official duties, I delight in sitting in meditation; rarely have I let my side touch the bed while sleeping. Although I now manifest as a ruler..."
The official’s appearance was dignified; his reputation as a venerable elder spread throughout the four seas. In the autumn of the twenty-third year of the Xiangshu era, he requested retirement.

He informed his relatives and acquaintances in advance, setting the third day of the tenth month as the date for his passing. On that day, he ordered a high seat to be set up in the rear hall and received visitors as usual.

Between the hours of Chén and Sì, he donned his ceremonial robes and cap, descended the steps, and performed a solemn prostration facing the imperial palace. He then invited the Commissioner of the Canal Administration.
He attended to the affairs of Qiong, donned his monastic robes and sandals, and sat upon a high seat.

He exhorted the officials and the clergy and laity, saying, "Each of you should turn toward the Way, support the teachings of the Gate, and establish the banner of the Dharma. Thereupon, he took up his staff, leaned it against his knee, and passed away with serene composure.
The Commissioner of the Circuit requested, "Your departure and arrival were so free and at ease; why not leave behind a verse? The Master opened his eyes and asked for paper.
He wrote in his calligraphy: "The first three and the eleventh; the middle nine and the lower seven. The old man’s words are exhausted; Guige’s eyes turn red.
Having finished writing, he passed away. After the Jianyan era, many collections of the Buddhist canon (*jiaozang*) were lost at famous mountains and great monasteries.
The Master repeatedly used his own stipend to print and distribute them, totaling one hundred twenty-eight sets. His disciple Pu Daping once recorded these events in an inscription.
There exists a collection of recorded sayings (*yulu*) and verses on ancient cases (*songgu*) that circulates in the world.
It was compiled by Zhang Jiucheng (who received the Dharma from Jingshan Hongzhao), a Minister of the Board of Rites during the Song dynasty.
Zhang Jiucheng, styled Zishao, was a native of Yanguan in Hangzhou; he was known as the Layman Wugou. He served in various official capacities, including the Ministry of Rites.

Shilang, before he had passed the imperial examinations, while conversing with a guest, mentioned that such Confucian scholars as Yang Wengong and Lü Weizhong had all attained realization through the study of Chan Buddhism, and thus he came to admire it deeply.
Upon hearing that Chan Master Baoyin Chuming’s teachings were derived from Dadao Tong and that he resided at Jingci Monastery, he went there to inquire about the essentials of entering the Way.
Chuming said, "In this matter, one must simply not abandon it for even a single thought-moment; after a long time of constant practice, it will naturally become mature."

When the critical moment arrives, one will naturally realize and enter [the truth]. He then brought up the story of Zhaozhou’s cypress tree, instructing him to keep it in mind and reflect upon it at all times.

After a long while, he still had no realization. He took his leave to visit Chan Master Qing of Shanguan, asking: "Is it not true that everyone has their share of this matter, and that each person achieves its full perfection?
Qing replied, "Indeed. The student asked, "Why is it that I have no point of entry? Qing reached into his sleeve and produced several...

Zhuzhu asked, "Whose is this? The official looked up and down, unable to respond. Qing then tucked it back into his sleeve and said, "If it is yours, then pick it up and take it away; as soon as you engage in thought, it is no longer yours. The official was struck with awe. Not long after, while staying at the residence of the Su family, he investigated the koan of the "cypress tree" one night while using the toilet. Upon hearing the croaking of frogs, he attained sudden enlightenment. There is [a verse]: The cypress tree stands in the courtyard, Its shadow falls upon the ground. When the moon shines through the window, The sound of the frogs fills the air. At that moment, the mind is suddenly liberated. No need to seek elsewhere—just look within. The thousand sages and ten thousand buddhas Are all contained within this single phrase. If you can grasp it here and now, You will see the ancient path clearly revealed. If you hesitate and fail to act, You will remain lost in the dark. Do not wait for another day— Right now, resolve it once and for all. This is the true meaning of the patriarchs’ transmission. It is not something to be found in books.

If you wish to enter the gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs, You must first understand this very point. If you can penetrate it in a single thought, You will transcend the world of birth and death. If you do not, you will continue to wander in delusion. Therefore, strive with all your might. Do not let this opportunity pass. This is the essential teaching of the Zen school. It is the direct pointing to the human heart. To realize it is to become a Buddha. To doubt it is to remain a common mortal. Take heed! Take heed! Do not waste your life in vain. This is the final instruction. May you all attain liberation. Thus ends the record.
The verse says: "A single frog’s cry on a spring night— It shatters heaven and earth; all share one family. At such a moment, who can understand?
Xuan Sha suffers aching feet at the mountain pass. On the following day, he went to visit Chan Master Fayan Yi. Their exchange of words was largely in accord.

It happened to be the anniversary of his private memorial service, so they held offerings at Mingjing Hermitage for the presiding monk, Weishang, and the assembly of monks. As soon as [Fayan] saw him, he extended [his hands].
Zhang Gong gave a shout. Weishang slapped him on the cheek. Gong stepped forward, and Weishang said, "How can you, Registrar Zhang, slander the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*?
Gong replied, "This is simply how my realization stands; what about you, Master? Weishang then cited the story of Mazu ascending the hall and Baizhang rolling up his mat to interrogate him:
(When Mazu ascended the hall and the assembly had just gathered, Baizhang came out and rolled up his mat; Mazu immediately descended from the seat.)
Before he had finished speaking, the Master pushed over the table. Weishang cried out, "Master Zhang, the Registrar, is murdering people!
The Master sprang up and asked a monk standing nearby, "What do you make of this? The monk was at a loss for words, so the Master struck him. Turning to Weishang, he said:

"When the ancestors do not settle their affairs, the calamity reaches their descendants. Weishang laughed heartily. Gong Xian offered this verse: "The circumstances of rolling up the mat are truly marvelous;
When all quarters hear it raised, they knit their brows. The stand and tray are kicked over and people scatter like stars;
A straightforward man has never suffered deception. Weishang replied: "From the beginning, I have set a high price and never yielded to him; Amidst the field of battle, he exerts himself."
The two eyebrows: seizing the corners and piercing the pass—do you understand? In the monastic forests, who would dare to deceive one another further?
In the *guichu* year of the Xiangxing era, after winning the highest honors among scholars, I again visited Weishang at Dong’an. Weishang said:
"Fushan Yuanjian said, 'Even if you were able to enter the chamber of Fenyang, you have only reached the gate of Fushan; you have still not seen the old monk. What do you say to this?"
The Duke rebuked an attendant monk, saying, "Why do you not respond directly? The monk was at a loss. The Duke struck the monk with his palm and said, "In a den of frogs, there truly is no dragon.
In the autumn of the Ding-si year, Da-hui presided over Mount Jing; scholars looked up to him as they do to the stars and constellations.

Lord Yue examined the essential points of his words and sighed, saying, "I knew there were people of the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen). He took this with him to tell Wei Shang, regretting that he had not yet met him in person.
Later, when Lord Yue served as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, he happened to visit Senior Statesman Liu Gong, who requested that Dahui preach the Dharma at Tianzhu Monastery.
Lord Yue went three times but did not meet him. When Dahui finally came to pay his respects, Lord Yue received him with nothing more than formal greetings. Dahui...
He also took this to heart in silence. Soon after, he returned to his home village to attend to ancestral sacrifices.

Upon reaching Mount Jing, he discussed the principle of "investigating things" (*gewu*) with Official Feng and several other gentlemen. Dahui said, "You only know 'investigating things,' but you do not know 'the investigation of things.

The official was utterly bewildered. Dahui laughed loudly. The official asked, "Can you explain this to me? Dahui replied, "Have you not seen it recorded in a minor collection of tales that a man of the Tang dynasty..."

Lu Xisheng was a native of Wú in Sūzhōu. During the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng, he was appointed as Tongzhōngshūménxià Píngzhāngshì (Chief Counselor of the Secretariat and Chancellery).
He once intended to visit the Chan Master Huìjì of Mount Yang; first, he drew this ○ seal and presented it for inspection. When Master Yang opened the seal, [he saw...]
The Governor issued a written decree stating: "To attain [the truth] without thinking falls into the second head; to attain it through thinking falls into the third head.
He then returned the document and sealed it back. When the Duke saw this, he entered the mountains. Yangshan came out to meet him at the gate. As soon as the Duke entered the gate, he asked:
"All three gates are open; which one shall we enter? Yangshan replied: "Enter through the Gate of Faith. Upon reaching the Dharma Hall, the Duke asked again.
"How is it when one does not exit the realm of Māra and immediately enters the realm of the Buddha? Yangshan pointed his whisk downward three times. The official then prostrated.
He asked again, "Does the Master maintain the precepts? Yangshan said, "I do not maintain the precepts. "Do you practice seated meditation?
Yangshan said, "I do not practice seated meditation. After a long silence, the official asked, "Do you understand? Yangshan said, "I do not understand."
Mount [Shishuang] said, "Listen to an old monk’s verse: Flowing along, I do not maintain the precepts; Stupefied, I do not sit in meditation.
Three or two bowls of strong tea— The meaning lies at the edge of the mattock. Yangshan then asked, "I have heard that you, Excellency, attained awakening through reading the sutras—is this true?
He replied, "Your disciple was reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* when I came across the passage: 'One enters nirvāṇa without severing afflictions.'"
"This is a place of peace and happiness. Yangshan held up his whisk and said, "As for this very thing, how does one enter? [Fazhen] replied, "'The word 'enter'—it is not even necessary.

Yangshan said, "'The word "enter" is not for you, Excellency. Fazhen then rose and departed. (Fazhen said: "Venerable sir, tell me, for what kind of person is the word 'enter'? Furthermore, Excellency, do not be vexed.")**
The Grand Tutor Wang Yanbin (who succeeded Changqing Leng in the Dharma), being a lay practitioner, invited Changqing to reside at Zhaoqing.
On the day of the opening of the hall, the official approached the corner of the dais in court attire and said, "I request the Master to preach the Dharma.
Changqing asked, "Do you hear it? The official prostrated himself. Changqing said, "Even so..."
It was thus. Fearing that someone might not agree, one day he entered the Buddha Hall at Zhaoqing and pointed to an almsbowl, asking the hall attendant, "What kind of bowl is this?
The attendant replied, "It is a Bhaiṣajyaguru bowl. The Master said, "I have only heard of the Dragon-subduing Bowl."
The abbot said, "I will wait for the dragon to descend. The Master said, "What if a cloud-grasping, wave-tossing [dragon] suddenly arrives? The abbot said, "He would not even look back.
The Master said, "Your words have fallen short" (Xuansha said, "Even with all your spiritual power, where could you run?";

Baofu said, "I take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha"; Baizhang constantly made the gesture of overturning a bowl; Yunmen said, "If you are born in heaven in a future life, do not let me down"). One day, as the Master entered the monastery, he saw a...
The gate was closed. Changqing asked Attendant Yan, "Is there anyone who would dare say that the Grand Master is present?
Yan replied, "Is there anyone who would dare say that the Grand Master is absent? Changqing said to Taifu, "Xuefeng held up his whisk to show the monks."
The monk then went out. "Based on this monk's conduct, he should have been called back and given a severe beating," the Master said.

Changqing asked, "What kind of mental state was that? The Master replied, "I almost let him off. Later, when the Master arrived at Zhaoqing to partake in tea, Upāsaka Lang and Mingzhao were holding the tea kettle.
Suddenly, the kettle tipped over. The Master asked, "What is beneath the tea stove? Lang replied, "Holding the stove."

The official said, "Since you are the deity who carries the incense burner, why did you overturn the tea? Lang said, "After serving an official for a thousand days, one may lose everything in a single morning.

The official brushed his sleeves and departed. Mingzhao said, "Venerable Lang has finished eating the meal at Zhaoqing, yet he goes outside to hunt wild roots. Lang asked, "How about you, Venerable? Mingzhao said, "A non-person."

He seized the opportunity. (Xuedou Xian said: "At that time, he should have simply kicked over the tea stove. He then offered this verse: "His coming to question was like a rising wind; his response was not skillful. How pitiable is the One-Eyed Dragon; he never once showed his fangs and claws.")
The fangs and claws are displayed like clouds and thunder; how many times has the wave against the current surged?
The Realized Man Lü Yan (who inherited the Dharma from Huanglong Ji), Realized Man Lü Yan, styled Dongbin, was a native of Jingzhao.
During the late Tang dynasty, he failed to pass the imperial examinations three times. One day, while in Chang’an...
He settled in a wine shop where he met Zhongli Quan, who bestowed upon him the art of prolonging life. From that time on, no one could fathom his origins.

Once, while traveling at Guizong on Mount Lu, he inscribed these words upon the wall of the bell tower: "A single day of pure leisure and self-mastery; The six spirits harmonized, bringing peace and security.
With the treasure within the *dantian*, there is no need to seek the Way; Facing objects without a mind, there is no need to inquire of Chan. Not long after, the Master... [passed away].
Passing through Huanglong Mountain, he beheld purple clouds forming a canopy and suspected there might be a person of extraordinary character.

He entered to pay his respects and encountered Huanglong striking the drum to ascend the hall. Recognizing that this was Master Lü, Huanglong wished to entice him forward and said in a stern voice, "Beside the seat is one who would steal the Dharma.
Lü stepped forth resolutely and asked: "Within a single grain of millet lies a world; within a half-measure of cooking pot..."
“Boiling mountains and rivers. He asked, “Tell me, what is the meaning of this? Huanglong pointed and said, “This is a corpse-guarding ghost.

Lü said, “But what can be done? I have in my bag the medicine of longevity and immortality. Huanglong said, “Even if it passes through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end it will surely fall into emptiness and oblivion.
Lü flew his sword to threaten him, but the sword could not penetrate. He then prostrated himself twice and requested instruction on the ultimate goal. Huanglong interrogated him, saying:
“Cooking mountains and rivers within a half-measure cauldron—this I do not ask. How is it that a single grain of millet contains a world?
At these words, Lü attained sudden realization and composed a verse, saying: “I have cast away my gourd-bag and smashed my lute; Now I no longer crave gold within the mercury.
Since first seeing Huanglong, I have finally realized all my former efforts were misplaced. Huanglong instructed him...

Jiagu (Supernatural Protection). [Alternative Record: The Immortal Lü encountered Chan Master Huanglong as the master ascended the seat. The master said, "There is someone in this assembly who steals the Dharma. Yan stepped forward and said, "Cloud-water Wayfarer. The master said, "When the clouds have vanished and the water has dried up, what then?"]
Yan Wudui asked. The Master answered on his behalf: "The Yellow Dragon has appeared. Later, he visited Chan Master Jue of Zhidu in Tanzhou, who said: "I traveled through Shaoguan and Chenzhou."
Traveling eastward down the Xiang River, I now met Master Jue. Observing him, his Chan practice was brilliant and refined, and the source of his nature was pure and pristine.

Sitting in quietude with knees pressed together, he withdrew his radiance to illuminate within. Aside from a single robe, he possessed no other clothing; aside from a single bowl, he had no other food.
One must reach the far shore of birth and death and shatter the shell of afflictions. Now, the Buddha’s robe is silent and its transmission has ceased;
the principles of Chan are remote and on the verge of extinction. Will it be our Master who shall support and revive them? I have composed this single quatrain as a record:

The enlightened one extends his heart to save all beings; Sages and worthies transmit the Dharma without departing from the Truth. I pray that you, Master, will explain the meaning of the Westward Journey.
As for the Seventh Patriarch, there has been no one [to succeed him] until now.

Prime Minister Wang Sui of the Song dynasty (who received the Dharma from Shoushan Nian)—Wang Sui, courtesy name Zizheng, was a native of Henan. Throughout his life, he admired the character of Pei Xiu and went to visit Shoushan.
Master Nian had attained the meaning beyond words; from that time on, he practiced it and gained a profound understanding of the Great Dharma.

When the Duke, serving as Minister of the Censorate, was dispatched to govern Qiantang, he went to visit Master Xiaoshou of Xingjiao Temple. Upon reaching the lake, he dismissed his retinue of attendants.

He walked alone up to the meditation hall. Shou was just then basking in the sun, wrapped in a coarse garment, appearing entirely unconcerned. Upon suddenly seeing him, he asked, "What is your surname, sir?
The official replied, "It follows my family name. Wang then bowed to him. Shou pushed aside his grass mat and sat upon the floor.

They conversed and laughed for the entire day before he departed. On another day, the official visited again; the monks of the temple struck the great bell loudly, and ten thousand fingers emerged to welcome him. However—

Shou hurried forward and stood beneath a pine tree. When the Duke saw him from afar, he stepped out of his carriage, took Shou’s hand, and said, "Why do you not come to meet me as you did on previous days?

Why have you suddenly adopted such formalities? Shou looked to his attendants and, walking along, remarked, "If the Vice Minister were to obtain [enlightenment] immediately, what would we do about the Chief Administrator's anger?
Both the Duke and Yang Dainian were renowned for having attained realization through Zen meditation.

Dadian compiled the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) in thirty fascicles. Master [Zhaojue] excised its redundancies and produced a fifteen-fascicle version titled the *Yuying ji* (Collection of Jade Blossoms).
At the time of his passing, he wrote this verse: The lamp in the painted hall has already been extinguished; To whom can I point my finger and speak? Coming and going are fundamentally ordinary;
The spring breeze sweeps away the lingering snow.
Song Xia Song (Successor to Fagu Yin Cong). Xia Song, courtesy name Ziqiao, was a native of De’an.

During the Huangyou era, he served as a Participant in State Affairs (*Canchizhengshi*). Regarding Master Guyin Cong, the Prime Minister found his words to accord with the essential pivot of the Dharma;
thus, he spent his days in the company of this venerable monk. Once, when Chan Master Shanglan Pu arrived, the Prime Minister questioned him:
"When the hundred limbs fall apart and scatter, which one is the Elder's own self? Pu said, "I left Qiyang on the twentieth day of last month;
you may go now. Pu, however, asked, "When the hundred limbs fall apart and scatter, which one is your honor’s own self?
Gong simply shouted. Pu said, "The shout is certainly not lacking, but after all, which one is your honor’s own self?"
The Master replied with a verse: "Cease trying to recognize the foremost pivot before the wind; where in the vast void can thought be lodged?
If this mountain monk wishes to convey the message, it is when the moon rises over ten thousand miles of cloudless sky. Fupo said, "This too is merely playing with the spirit."
The Layman Li Duanyuan, Military Commissioner of Song (who inherited the Dharma from Jinshan Ying):
When he was a child in the state guest-house, he frequently read Chan texts; although he later married and entered official service, [he remained devoted to the Way].
However, being resolute in his commitment to the ancestral Way, he subsequently built a dwelling in his rear garden that resembled an *ārāma* (monastery) and invited Daguan to reside there.

Morning and evening, he consulted and studied with him, forgetting even to sleep or eat. One day, Daguan looked at the Master and said, "Were it not for the power of manifesting [through skillful means], how could you have reached this state?
Alas, what place of entry do you lack? The Master asked, "Are heaven and hell ultimately real, or are they not?"
"No. "Please, Master, explain this clearly. Daguang said: "The Buddhas speak of existence within non-existence; it is like seeing flowers in the sky with one's own eyes.

Your Excellency seeks non-existence within existence; it is like grasping at the moon reflected in water. It is truly laughable that you see a prison before your eyes yet do not avoid it, while hearing of heaven beyond your mind and desiring to be born there.
You fail to realize that joy and fear reside in the mind, and that good and evil constitute the external environment. Your Excellency should simply—"
"Once you have realized your own mind, naturally there will be no delusion. The Duke asked, "How does one realize the mind? Daguan said, "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all.
The Duke asked, "After one ceases to deliberate, where does the mind go? Daguan said, "Please, Commissioner, return to your residence for now.
The Duke asked, "As for when a person dies, where does the mind go? Daguan said, "If you do not yet know life, how can you know death?"

[The Master] died. The Duke said, "As for life, I already understand it. Daguan asked, "From where does life come? The Duke was at a loss. Daguan rose, thrust his hand toward the Duke’s chest, and said, "It is right here. What more do you intend to ponder? The Duke said, "I have understood. Daguan asked, "How do you understand? The Duke said, "I only knew how to hasten on my journey; I did not realize I had missed the way. Daguan said, "You have indeed understood. The Duke said, "I have understood. Guantuo opened his eyes and said, "A hundred-year dream—only this morning have I finally awakened. He then spoke a verse: "At thirty-eight years of age, I was oblivious and ignorant.
Now that I possess awareness, how am I any different from my former ignorance? The waters of the Bian River flow on; the embankments of Sui remain faintly visible.
Master, you shall return home; the arrow-like waves rush eastward."
Song Dynasty Grand Preceptor Gao Shize (who succeeded Fuyong Kai):
Grand Preceptor Gao Shize, courtesy name Zhongyi, styled Mugong. Initially, he attended Chan Master Fuyong Kai to seek instruction on the essential point of the mind.
Fuyong instructed him to set aside what he valued and to investigate by turning inward. One day, he suddenly penetrated the subtle and profound. He presented [his realization].
The verse says: Letting go over the precipice, one moves freely in all directions; the great earth and empty space are naturally level and plain.
Illuminating the ravines and shining upon the crags without borrowing from the moon, there is another screen of light within the hermitage.
Xu Shi (who succeeded Dongshan Cong in the Dharma), the Governor of Song.
Xu Shi was the Governor of Hongzhou. He attended upon Chan Master Dongshan Cong and attained the Eye of the True Dharma.
One day, while sitting with Letai Cheng and Shanglan Pu, Letai asked: "I have heard, Langzhong, that you said: 'Sitting at night upon the Cloud-Connected Stone.'"
"Planting pines in spring while it rains. At that time, what was he answering Dongshan? The Master said, "The office has been dismissed early today.
Letan asked, "I heard you answered that the Great Sage of Sizhou appears in Yangzhou—is that so?
The Master said, "Serve another cup of tea. Letan said, "His reputation is not in vain. The Master said, "When will you, Master, return to the mountain? Letan—
[The Master] said, "Today you were seen through by Shanglan. Shanglan then gave a shout. Letan said, "It must be you who achieves this.
The Master said, "What can one do with the boat? I shall break the scoop. The Master entered Shanglan’s monks’ hall and asked the Head Seat, "How many years of age are you?
[He] replied, "Sixty-eight. The Master said, "How many years of monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) do you have? [He] replied, "Forty-seven summer retreats. The Master said, "The Sage..."

"How many summer retreats has the Sangha attained? he asked. [The monk] replied, "He received the precepts simultaneously with empty space. The Official struck the wooden board and said, "As for this subordinate eating rice, it is not like the Head Seat eating so much salt.

[Appendix: When Xu Shi was serving as the Transport Commissioner in Western Shu, he went to visit Guanghui Lian. It happened that they met before the Buddha. The Official said, "Should one first bow to the Buddha, or first bow to the Elder?

Guanghui said, "A shrimp swallows a large tiger. The Official said, "If that is so, then we shall not bow at all. Guanghui said, "The Commissioner has fallen into error in his speech. The Official said, "Elder Xu possesses a single eye. Guanghui then brushed him away with his sleeve.]
Xu said, "Today I have seen through it," and he immediately prostrated.

Zeng Hui, the Song Dynasty Court Editor (who received the Dharma from Xuedou Xian), whose courtesy name was Zongyuan, served as the Hanlin Academician. In his youth, he had been a fellow student with Chan Master Mingjue Xian.
When they reached adulthood and took their separate paths, during the Tianxi era, while the Master was serving as the governor of Chizhou, he once encountered [Zhao] at Jingde Temple.

The Master then cited the *Zhongyong* and the *Daxue*, supplementing them with the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and correlating them with the sayings of the Chan school to examine [Zhao]'s understanding. Mingjue said:
"This [teaching] does not even accord with the scriptural vehicles (śāsana), let alone the *Zhongyong* or the *Daxue*. Scholar, you must understand this matter through a direct and swift path.
Then, snapping his fingers once, he said, "Just realize it in this way! The official attained the essential meaning beneath these words.
At the beginning of the Tiānshèng era, when the Duke was governing Sìmíng, he sent letters and gifts to invite the Master to take up the post at Xuědòu.
Once the Master had arrived, the Duke said, "Recently, I discussed the 'Old Woman' koan with Elder Qīng; I do not know for certain whether there is a point where she is truly exposed.
Míngjué asked, "What did Elder Qīng say? The Duke replied, "He just went off like that. Míngjué [laughed].
He said, "Elder Qing has let one move pass. Does the scholar still know that the monks of the world cannot escape this old woman’s snare?
The Duke said, "There is another way here. If Zhaozhou had not exposed her, she would have suffered a lifelong injustice. Mingjue said, "She has been exposed. The Duke laughed heartily.
The State Councilor of the Song Dynasty, Fu Bi (who inherited the Dharma from Touzi Yong), was a lay practitioner.
His courtesy name was Yanguo. Initially, he had not yet found his direction within the Chan school. Qu Qingxian Gong Biao exhorted him, saying:
"I humbly observe that Your Excellency’s wealth and honor have reached such an extreme, yet your cultivation of the Way and virtue remains thus..."
His fortune, longevity, well-being, and peace are thus fully provided; his retirement and leisure are thus sublime.

Yet, that which he has not yet paid sufficient attention to is nothing other than the Tathāgata’s single great cause and condition. May he be able to seek with single-minded sincerity that which is to be realized and awakened.

Thus, on another day, he went to offer congratulations at the Gate (the master’s residence). After being exhorted by Qingxian, the Duke applied himself to this Way with diligence, never ceasing day or night.
Hearing that Chan Master Yong presided over Touzi and that his Dharma assembly was preeminent throughout the Huaidian region, the Duke went there to resolve his doubts.
When Huiyong ascended the seat for the assembly, Fan Gong observed that his gaze was like the turning of an elephant king. Gong felt he had attained something;

he therefore performed the rites of a disciple, approached the master’s quarters, and ordered an attendant to request admittance into the inner chamber. As soon as Huiyong saw him, he said, "The Minister has already entered; Fu Bi is still outside.
Upon hearing this, Gong broke into a sweat that drenched his back, and he attained great enlightenment immediately thereafter. He subsequently composed a verse: [Verse omitted per instructions]
He sent a letter to Yuanzhao, saying: "Upon seeing Master Yong once, my realization was profound; through successive conditions, I have transmitted the heart-mind of the Old Teacher.

Though people in the southeast may speak of the vast distance of rivers and mountains, I face the *lingguang* (numinous light) and the *miaoyin* (wondrous sound) directly before my eyes. Later, he submitted a memorial requesting the posthumous title for Master Yong.
When Yong ascended the hall to express his gratitude, he said: "That was a one-time error on their part; I too shall follow the error with an error. Gong composed [the following]:
The verse of praise says: Ten thousand trees and a thousand flowers desire to flourish, yet the Dragon Reclining has not yet emerged from the vast ocean.
Auspicious omens appear in crimson clouds and colored mists; as before, the Southern Mountain remains a single color of green.
Dai Fu Wang of Wei Prefecture in the Song dynasty (his posthumous name was Sifa Yuanfeng Man).
Dai Fu Wang’s personal name is lost to history. Having lost his wife, he grew weary of the phenomena of the world and subsequently attended upon Yuanfeng.
Under Yuanfeng’s instruction, he realized his ultimate destination. One day, Yuanfeng said to him, "You are the Lu Xuan of the present age. The Master immediately covered his ears.

Thereafter, he returned to the southern slope of Mount Tan and dwelt there, sheltering himself in a thatched hut, for three years. He happened to sing: “How long is the day within the folds of Mount Tan!
The green pines on the ridges, the white clouds of my native land. Chanting birds and crying monkeys serve as my place of practice;
I loosen my hair, gather ferns, and sing again with laughter. Let people call me a wild man mad—what does it matter?”
The Imperial Historian Huang Tingjian (who received the Dharma from Huanglong Xin), known as the Layman Shangu, was styled Lüzhi.
Possessing the karmic predispositions of past lives for Prajñā, he remained detached despite holding high office.
Although he frequented various Zen lineages, he had not yet found his true direction; he was fond of composing flowery verses and once visited Yuan Tong Xiu.
Chan Master Xiu scolded him, saying, "A man of such stature—how can you be content to expend your mastery of calligraphy upon this?
At that time, Xiu was instructing Li Bashi on the matter of painting horses. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Are you not about to place me once again within the belly of a horse?
Xiu replied, "You stir up the lustful hearts of all people under heaven with your flowery words; it is not merely the horse's belly I fear, but rather that you will be born in the mud."
Lier heard this and was struck with awe; he repented and apologized. From then on, he ceased his literary pursuits and devoted himself solely to the Way.

He composed a text on making vows and strictly refrained from alcohol and sensual indulgence, taking only morning gruel and midday meals. He went to rely upon Huìtáng, requesting instruction on the direct and expedient path.
Huìtáng said, "As for Confucius saying, 'Disciples, do you think I am hiding anything from you? I hide nothing from you,' how would you explain this when in your ordinary state?
When the Master (Gōng) was about to offer a reply, Huìtáng said, "Not so, not so. The Master remained in a state of confusion and distress.
One day, while they were walking in the mountains, the rock-orchids were in full bloom. Huìtáng said, "I smell the magnolia."
"Does the flower have fragrance? The official replied, "I smell it. Huitang said, "I have hidden nothing from you.
The official was suddenly relieved and prostrated himself, saying, "How earnest is the Master’s compassionate heart! Huitang smiled and said, "I only wish for you to arrive home."
At that time, the Duke had recently begun to enter the path. He asked Huitang, "Who here is capable of engaging in dialogue with me?
Huitang replied, "Quán of Zhāngzhōu. Thereupon, he went together with Huitang to see Quán. At that moment, Quán was supervising laborers as they were reclaiming land for cultivation.
The Duke said, "Does the steward know that the pillar has given birth to a child? Quán asked, "Is it a boy or a girl? As the Duke hesitated, Quán struck him. Huitang then said to him:
"One must not be discourteous. Quan said, "This block of wood—if I do not strike him, when shall I wait for the time?

The official laughed heartily. After some time, he went to visit the Chan Master Xin of Yunyan. Following the assembly, they entered the inner quarters. Upon seeing him, Xin opened his eyes wide and asked, "The Elder Xin has died;
you, Scholar, have died. Once burned into two heaps of ash, in what place will we meet? The official was speechless.

Sishin Yuochu said: "What you attained while under Huichang has not yet truly taken root. Later, after being demoted to office and tattooed in the south, your power of the Way grew even more superior.
Amidst a state of non-thought, you suddenly clarified what Sishin had asked. He sent a letter in reply, saying:

'In years past, I was constantly favored by your persistent prodding and reminders, yet for a long time I remained as if in a drunken dream, with things appearing only vaguely within a realm of light and shadow; this was because of my lingering doubt.'"
"It is not yet exhausted; because the life-root (*jīvitendriya*) has not been severed, I merely retreated out of regard for the precipice.
While in exile in the region south of the Qíng Mountains, he woke from a nap and suddenly reflected: "How much have I been deceived by the old monks of the world?
Only the monk Sīnmén (Dead Heart) refused to comply; that was truly the foremost act of true concern for me. Later, he composed the epitaph for Huìtáng, saying: "I, [Name]..."

Having long ago received the transmission of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), you were capable of upholding the Great Dharma. Yet, as your eye of the Way was not yet fully perfected, you have come to gaze upon this stūpa;
truly, this evokes a profound sigh of veneration and admiration. Thus, I have inscribed these words upon firm stone to respectfully eulogize your remaining virtues.

The Master further prepared an offering of simple greens and wild plants, sacrificing with a prose text and consoling with a verse, which says: "The wind of the sea blows down Mount Laṅkā; The Chan practitioners of the four seas must now open their eyes."
Look! A tangle of willow threads cannot be gathered; together with the mist, they lean against the jade balustrade.
Wang Shao (Sishfa Huanglong Xin), State Councilor Guanwen.
The layman Wang Shao, courtesy name Zichun, was dispatched as the Governor of Hongzhou. He then invited Chan Master Huidang to inquire [about the Dharma].
Dao silently attained a realization of accord and thereupon composed a verse on seizing the opportune moment, saying: "By day I forgot to eat; by night I forgot to sleep.
Holding the dragon pearl, I wished to ascend to heaven. Yet I cast it all down within my own self; The four corners lie flat upon the ground, perfectly round.
Huītáng deeply approved of this.
Wu Xun (who inherited the Dharma from Huanglong Xin), Secretariat of the Song Dynasty.
Wu Xun’s courtesy name was Defu; he served as an official in the Secretariat. While residing at Huìtáng, he entered the inner sanctum [of the master].
Huìtáng said to him, “I shall not ask about your lifelong studies, intellectual understanding, memory, or extensive learning. Tell me this: before your parents were born, speak one word.”

The phrase was brought forward. As the Master (Gong) was about to deliberate upon it, Heitang struck him with his whisk. At that moment, he grasped the profound meaning and presented a verse, saying: "Ha!
This knowledgeable worldly fellow has gnawed through all the public cases of the past and present. Suddenly, from amidst a heap of filth, he picked up a dung ball of a dung beetle.
It is perfectly clear and not worth a single cent; ten thousand taels of gold would not exchange for it. He has casually brought it forth."
He showed it to the people, saying: "It is simply because the 'running plate' is difficult to behold. Heh! Huìtáng replied: 'To find fire within water is rare in this world;
looking upon it makes one especially suspicious. From of old, there have been no masters or disciples; now, however, we allow the Old Barbarian to know. (Jiǎofàn’s *Línjiān Lù* states:

There was a layman named Wú Dūnfú, who was talented and sharp-witted, and was resolute in his pursuit of the Way. Believing himself to have seen many spiritual teachers and possessing a clear and pure mind, he happened to read the biography of Dèng Yǐnpéng and saw that he had passed away while standing upside down.)

Yet his robe remained draped over his body without slipping down. Dunfu privately marveled at this, thinking: "The wonders of his supernatural transformations are indeed unfathomable, but why does his robe also conform to him? He asked the Elder Huitang about this. Huitang said, "Now your own robe hangs down to the ground; do you have any doubt about that? Dunfu replied, "I have no doubt.

Huitang laughed and said, "If you have no doubt about this, then why should you doubt that when he transformed into an inverted tree, his robe likewise conformed to his body? What is there to doubt? At these words, Dunfu attained understanding.
Thus, his spontaneous and timely eloquence was like thunder or a clap of lightning, awakening and warning many who were mired in ignorance and delusion.
Su Shi (Sishifa Donglin Zong), Inner Secretary of the Song Dynasty.
Su Shi, styled Zizhan, stayed overnight at Donglin Temple and engaged in a discussion on the "discourse of the insentient" with Zhaojue. He attained realization and, at dawn, offered this verse:
"The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; The color of the mountains is surely the pure and serene body. Last night, [the Buddha]..."

"Fourteen thousand stanzas—how could one possibly present them to others on another day? (The Dharma Master Wuzhuo of India visited Chan Master Cigan Yuan. During their conversation at night, the Master cited the verse by Dongpo on staying at Donglin:

"It is not easy to reach such a state. Cigan said, "You have not yet even seen the path; how can you speak of 'reaching' it? Wuzhuo said, "As for what he said: 'The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; the color of the mountains is surely the pure body.

If one had not reached this state, how could there be such a message? Cigan said, "That is merely a man from outside the gate. Wuzhuo said, "If the Master will not be stingy, please explain it for me. Cigan said, "Then you must simply apply yourself with fierce diligence right here.")

He scrutinized and investigated him. If he could scrutinize and capture his [the opponent's] breakdown, then he would also know where his own *mūlādhāra* (vital point) was situated. The Master did not sleep all night. When the bell rang at dawn, he removed his secret provisions and addressed him with a previous verse, saying:

"The Layman Dongpo is far too talkative; he wishes to pass through the barrier of sound and form. If the stream is sound and the mountain is form, then without mountain and without water, one is a person for whom there is only sorrow. He specifically told this to Ch'an-kan. Ch'an-kan said, "I told you before that you are a man from outside the gate.

He spoke again: "Seen from the front, it forms a ridge; seen from the side, it forms a peak. Looking at the mountains everywhere, they are nowhere the same. One does not recognize the true face of Mount Lu."
His face and features were such that it was simply because he was within the mountains. Before long, he arrived at Jingnan.
Hearing that the Chan Master Haoyuquan’s sharp spiritual edge (*jīfēng*) was unassailable, the Official intended to suppress him; he therefore disguised his appearance and sought an audience.
Yuquan asked, "What is your honorable surname? The Official replied, "My surname is Scale (*chèng*). This was the scale used to weigh the elders of the world. Yuquan shouted, "Now tell me, this—"

"How heavy is this one shout? Gong had no reply; thereupon, he paid him profound respect. (Chushi Qi said: "Yuanquan was a master craftsman of the school, and Dongpo was a great Confucian scholar of his time.

Meeting head-on, they brought forth this Way. Everyone says that Dongpo withdrew, as if the scale had no stars; yet they do not realize that eight *liang* and half a *jin* are both in one's own hands.

Nevertheless, even so, he helped Yuanquan up. As for his question, 'How heavy is this one shout? how many people could not answer? Even if one could answer, one would still give another shout. Gong was banished to Huangzhou, while Foyin resided [at Mount Lu].
Guihong of Mount Lu was a friend in the Way beyond formal boundaries. When Foyin moved to reside at Jinshan, the Duke (Wang Anshi) was released from his confinement.

While serving as the Governor of Hangzhou, he passed by Jinshan and happened upon Foyin entering his room for meditation. The Duke nevertheless went to visit him. Foyin said, "There is no place here to sit."
The Duke said, "I would temporarily borrow the Venerable’s four elements as a meditation seat. Foyin replied, "There is a turning phrase;
if you can answer it, I shall grant your request. If you hesitate, however, I shall keep the jade belt you have fastened. The Duke immediately placed the belt upon a table.
Foyin said, "The four elements of this mountain monk are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist. Where, then, would you, Inner Secretary, wish to sit?
As the official hesitated, Foyin called to his attendant, saying, "Take this jade belt and let it remain forever to adorn the mountain gate.

Later, when the official passed through Mount Jin, there was someone painting his portrait. He playfully inscribed upon it: "My mind is like wood whose fire has long been extinguished; my body is like..."
An unmoored boat asks you about your lifelong achievements: Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Qiongzhou.
Su Che, the State Councilor of the Song Dynasty (who received the Dharma from Shanglan Shun), was a lay practitioner.
His courtesy name was Ziyou. In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, he was demoted from his position as an official in Suizhou.
While he was serving as the tax collector for Ruizhou, Chan Master Shun of Shanglan in Hongzhou happened to visit him, as he shared a spiritual affinity with his father, Mr. Wen’an.

They met with great joy, and the official consulted the master regarding the Dharma of the mind. Shun showed him the karmic cause and condition of "pinching the nose," after which the official attained realization.
He composed a verse to present to the master, saying: "In middle age I heard the Way and realized my former errors. By chance..."
Meeting by chance, I encountered Master Lǎoshùn; pinching my nose, I directly sought his true countenance. Shaking my head, I refused any further tongs or hammers.
What is this withered vine and tattered robe? Who am I, amidst the white wine and green salt? I am ashamed before the waning moon over the eastern eaves;
a single cup of nectar-like ambrosia is as smooth as honey.
Dai Daochun (Successor to Huanglong Qing), Court Vice Minister of the Song Dynasty.
Dai Daochun, courtesy name Fuzhong, held the office of Court Vice Minister. He sought instruction from Lingyuan and attained realization one day, whereupon he presented this verse:
"At the bottom of the profound and dark source, where the total function resides, A single flower of mind reveals the pattern of the seal. I know that for many lifetimes..."
He made offerings. From time to time, he smiled, causing clouds of incense to stir.
Regarding Wen-ding Duke Hu An-guo (Sishfa Shangfeng Xiù):
Wen-ding Duke Hu An-guo, courtesy name Kanghou, with the sobriquet Cao’an Jushi, long relied upon Shangfeng Xiù.
The Chan Master had attained the meaning beyond words. During the Chongning era, he visited Yaoshan. There, a practitioner raised the story of Nanquan’s beheading of the cat to question him.
The Master replied with a verse: "In hand, he holds the pivot of life and death for heaven and earth; His arrangements and displays are applied according to the moment.
The jade hall, the rabbit, and the horse are not dragons or elephants; In his majestic great function, they are all utterly unknown. He also sent this [verse] upward:
The Inscription on Fengyou Peak reads: The Peak of Zhurong resembles the heavens above Duche City; Ten thousand ages of rivers and mountains are present before one's eyes.
One must believe that the Dead Heart has never truly died; Last night, the autumn moon was once again full together with it.
Fan Chong (Successor to the Dharma of Master Mantian of Yuan Tong), Vice President of the Secretariat of the Song Dynasty.

His courtesy name was Qianshu; he was also known as Zhixu. While serving as the Governor of Yuzhang from his post in the Han-yuan (the Imperial Academy), he visited Chan Master Mantian of Yuan Tong and said:
"I am approaching old age. What kind of karmic practice did I perform in my past lives? Why have I been born this time within the ranks of the 'Golden and Purple' (the high nobility)?"

[The Master] was in the middle [of his journey]. This matter was somewhat distant from him. Yuantong called out, "Director of the Hanlin Academy! The Master responded, "Yes? Yuantong said, "How can there be any distance?
The Master leaped up in joy and said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction. Yuantong said, "From here to Hongdu, it is four stages' journey.

The Master stood in thought for a moment. Yuantong said, "If you see it, you see it immediately; if you deliberate upon it, you have already missed it. Thereupon, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
Preface. Wu Juhou (who inherited the Dharma from Yuan Tong Min), Chief Secretary of State during the Song Dynasty.
Holding his ceremonial staff, Wu Juhou returned to Zhongling. He paid a visit to Chan Master Yuan Tong Min and said: "I, [your disciple], have recently..."
He was traveling to the provincial examination when he arrived at Zhaozhou’s Barrier. There, he asked the former resident, Old Ne, about the matter of penetrating the barrier.

Ne said, "Go ahead and take office for now. Today, more than fifty years have passed without his even realizing it. Yuancong asked, "Have you ever clearly understood the matter of penetrating the barrier?
Gong replied, "I have passed through it eight times, always keeping this thought in mind, yet I have not yet attained a state of complete liberation."
When Yuan Tong was fanning himself, he said to the official, "Please, let me fan you. The official immediately waved the fan.
Yuan Tong said, "What is there that is not refreshing? The official suddenly attained realization and said, "Then please grant me the final word.
Yuan Tong then waved the fan twice. The official said, "Intimate! Intimate! Yuan Tong replied, "The tongue of this barbarian reaches three thousand li."
Peng Rulin (Successor to the Dharma of Yuantong Min), Counselor-in-Waiting of the Song Dynasty.
Peng Rulin held the office of Counselor-in-Waiting. He had handwritten a copy of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra to offer to Yuantong.
Yuantong picked it up and said, "This is the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra; which one is the Counselor’s sūtra? The official replied, "This was written by me with my own hand. Yuantong—

[The official] said, "This is the written copy; which one is the sūtra? Yuancong laughed and said, "That would not do. [The official] said, "Even while manifesting in the body of a lay official, you preach the Dharma. Yuancong said, "Do not slander the sūtra. [The official] asked, "How is it so? Yuancong held up the sūtra to show him. Yuancong asked, "What is the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West? Layman Pang replied, "The blue sky is clear and bright. Yuancong said, "You have already been through this before. Layman Pang said, "I am not deceiving you. Yuancong said, "If you are not deceiving me, why did you come here? Layman Pang said, "To pay my respects to the Master.
