(Lu Hang, the Governor of Zhong, who received the Dharma from Yuan-tong Min; Lu Hang held the office of Zhongcheng.
While he was warming himself by the brazier with Yuan-tong, the official asked: "There is no need to trouble yourself with the karmic conditions of the various houses."
[Zhaozhou] brought it forth: "A direct, single phrase—please, Master, point it out for me. Yuantong pointed at him with a stern voice, saying, "Look at the fire!
Zhaozhou hurriedly pulled back his robe and suddenly attained great enlightenment. He bowed in thanks, saying, "Clearly, there is not much to this Buddha-dharma after all.
Yuantong shouted, "Put it down! Zhaozhou responded, "Yes, yes."

Du Xiang (who succeeded to the Dharma of Yuan Tong Min), serving as the Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs, asked Yuan Tong: "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought, deliberation, or discrimination."
"How should one settle this? Yuan Tong said, "Enter the mass of fire with your whole body. The official asked, "Ultimately, how does one understand this?
Yuan Tong said, "Go straight ahead. The official hesitated. Yuan Tong said, "Would you like some tea? The official replied, "Yes."
"Not necessary," Yuan-tong said. "Why do you not understand it in this way? The Master (Gong) attained the essential meaning and said, "It turns out to be far too near.
Yuan-tong said, "The hundred thousand and eight thousand [miles]. The Master then offered this verse: "Inconceivable! This is a great mass of fire.
To go thus, one does not leave this very place. Yuan-tong said, "Ei! There is still this thing remaining. The Master said, "I beg the Master to bestow [further instruction] once more."
The Master pointed his finger and said, "If you go about in this very way, the cauldron is cast of iron. The official bowed his head in thanks.

The layman Sun of the Ministry of Rites (who succeeded Yangqi Hui in the Dharma) was visiting when Chan Master Yangqi Hui arrived. It happened that the official was presiding over a legal case when he said, "I..."
"Dragged away by royal affairs, by what means can I escape them? Yangqi pointed and said, "Do you understand thoroughly? The official said, "I hope the Master will clarify this for me.
Yangqi said, "This is the profound and vast vow of the Minister of Rites (Bibù) to benefit all living beings. The official said, [I do not understand]."
Not knowing what this meant, Yangqi showed him with a verse: “Manifesting in the body of a high official, The compassionate vow is extensively propagated and profound.
For the sake of people, he points out the place once more: Beneath the staff, blood flows profusely. At these words, the official attained realization.
Guo Xiangzheng (Successor to Baiyun Wenda), Provincial Judicial Commissioner of Song.

Guo Xiangzheng, courtesy name Gongfu, was a native of Dangtu. He styled himself the Layman Jingkong. His official rank reached that of Palace Attendant. He resigned from office and lived in seclusion at Qingshan.
Once, while crossing the river, he went to pay his respects to Chan Master Baiyun Wenda of Shuzhou. The Master ascended the hall and said:
Last night, while upon my pillow, I composed this mountain verse to express my gratitude to Mr.

Gōngfǔ, the Great Scholar, for his twenty years of friendship with Mount Lúshān and his diligent journey from afar today to visit Báiyún. You must recite it for the assembly so that, hereafter, it may be clearly presented to all quarters.
This verse is not merely to thank Mr. Gōngfǔ; it is intended to reach all those throughout the world who possess nostrils.
The monk Kongna said, "Take off your flesh-colored undershirt; do not say I did not tell you. He then recited: "The Great Man of Shang, Qiu Yiji;
he transformed three thousand and seventy scholars. You, little students, eight or nine of you; well-composed and benevolent, you may know the rites."
The Duke was deeply perplexed. Later, upon hearing a child reciting [the verse], he suddenly attained realization. He wrote a letter to Baoyun to report this. Baoyun replied with a verse:
"To hide one's body, there is no need to shrink the head; To conceal one's traces, why must one draw back the feet?
The golden crow soars through the vast heavens at midnight; The jade hare cannot catch up to him. One day, Baoyun asked, "Is the ox pure? The Duke replied, "It is pure."
Baoyun scolded him. The Master stood with his hands folded in reverence. Baoyun said, "How pure! How pure! Nanquan and Dayue were no different from this.
He then presented him with a verse: "The ox comes into the mountains; water is sufficient, grass is sufficient. The ox leaves the mountains; [the tracks] remain."
"Touching east, touching west. During the Yuanyou era, he went to Nanchan in Quzhou to pay his respects to Master Quan Wanjuan and requested to ascend the seat.

The Master stepped forward, offered incense, and said: "A withered tree by the sea, once it enters my hands, becomes incense. When burned in the burner, it pierces horizontally through the nostrils of the Incense Accumulation Tathāgata.
To accomplish such a great matter, one must first announce it before the assembly. Thus spoke the Old Master of Yunju.
A person possesses a seamless robe, which was entrusted to Chan Master Nanchan. When he put it on, it was neither too long nor too short;
advancing, all Buddhas yielded their thrones; retreating, the waves of the sea became calm. Today, with a single sigh, the six kinds of earth tremors occurred.
He then called out, "Great assembly, do you understand? When one has spirit, one adds to that spirit; when one lacks elegance..."
He was a man of refined elegance. Quan said, "We have been mutually neglectful of one another. The Duke asked, "By whom was this brought about?

At the beginning of the Chongning era, he went to Dongshan in Huangmei and invited Master Yan to preach the Dharma. The Duke stepped forward, held up the incense, and said, "This single offering of incense..."
I burn incense before the brazier to make offerings to my Dharma brother, the Zen Master of this Hall.

I prostrate myself and pray that, from the seat of the Vast and Perfect, you will part the face of your countenance and manifest the physical form (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*) of our late teacher for all people to depict. Why must it be so?
We met long ago on the cliffs of White Cloud; The matters of those days and today are not the same. The night is still and the water cold, yet the fish do not bite.
A single incense burner scatters fragrance upon White Lotus Peak. The Patriarch then said: *Namo satvata paraya*.
"In this way, in this way"—how many times have I gazed upon the white clouds above the mountain stream? The yellow plum blossoms open amidst the snow.
"Not in this way, not in this way"—tender willows hang down golden threads; one must simply respond to the season. Have you not seen how Layman Pang asked Master Ma?
The Master said: "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion? The Great Master replied:

"Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River in a single mouth, and then I will tell you. O assembly, to suck up all the water of the West River in a single mouth is to reach the very bottom of a ten-thousand-fathom deep abyss.
This rickety footbridge is no bridge of Zhaozhou; how can bright moon and clear breeze compare? Hereafter...
He then went to Baoning Temple, where he was also invited to ascend the seat. The Master held up the incense and said, "The Dharma drum has been struck and the precious incense has just been lit;
at the gate of Yangqi’s head, I request the Master to drive in the wedge once more. Baoning struck his staff once and said, "The wedge has been driven in;
the assembly bears witness. He struck it once again and then descended from the seat. He then went to Yunju Temple, where he invited Foyin.
He ascended the seat. The Master held up the incense and said: "Meeting on the ground of awakening—how early! The foul-smelling monk’s robe is now cast off.
If you wish to recognize the one mysterious word of Yunju, take care: the donkey is eating grass in the back garden. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"This single offering of incense rises to scorch the heavens and sear the earth. Foyin remarked: "Today he has no choice but to yield; he has been caught by this fellow."
He smeared his face with paste and struck [the monk], saying: "Thank you, sir, for coming a thousand li to visit me. Together we shall speak of the deep bamboo path on Mount Dongshan.
I lend you a dragon to ride out of the cave; should you encounter a drought, let it bring down the rain. He then threw down his staff and descended from his seat.
The Duke bowed and rose. Foyin asked, "Have you caught the dragon? The Duke said, "It is already here. Foyin asked, "How do you ride it? The Duke made a waving gesture, danced, and departed.
Foyin clapped his hands and said, "Only this fellow has some measure of comparison.

[Commentary: Chan Master Ke Xuan of Guizong in Jiangzhou was on friendly terms with Guo Gongfu. When the Master took charge of Guizong, Gongfu was serving as the Commandant of Nanchang. Shortly thereafter, the Prefect became resentful because the Master did not pay him formal courtesy. [He sought to find fault with him.]

"Indeed. He then wrote a letter to Gongfu, saying: "My worldly karmic ties still have six years remaining. However, as the Prefectural Governor has pressured me, I must cast off my remaining breaths to take rebirth in your household. I pray you will not obstruct this. When Gongfu read the letter, he was both surprised and delighted, and he accepted it. In the middle of the night, his wife saw the Master enter her bedchamber in a dream;

she cried out in alarm, "This is not where the Monk comes from! Gongfu shook her awake and questioned her. She told him everything in detail. He called for a lamp and showed her the letter; they laughed together without ceasing, and she subsequently became pregnant.

When he was born, they named him Xuān-lǎo. At one year of age, his memory and responses were as they had been before. When he reached three years old, Băiyún Chāndé arrived at his home and first saw him, saying, "My nephew has come! Băiyún asked, "How many years have passed since we parted from you, Master?

Xuān counted back on his fingers and said, "Four years. Băiyún asked, "Where did we part? He replied, "At the Bái-lián Estate. Băiyún asked, "What is your proof? He said, "Father and Mother. [Xuān] then invited the Master for a meal the following day. Suddenly, they heard the sound of a cart being pushed. Băiyún asked, "What is that sound outside the gate?
Xuān made a gesture with his hand as if pushing a cart. Băiyún asked, "What happens after it passes? He replied, "Two ruts in level ground. Indeed, at the age of six, he passed away without illness.
Prince Zhao Lingjin (Successor to the Dharma of Zhaojue Qin), Prince of Song.
His courtesy name was Biaozhi, and his style name was Chao’ran Jushi. He was a fifth-generation descendant of Emperor Taizu.

While serving as the governor of Nankang, his administration was successful and affairs were few; he frequently associated with Chan monks. Within his official hall, he established a chamber for Māghata (Vimalakīrti). Just then, Yuan... [text ends]
Chan Master Wuzu arrived at Mount Ou in accordance with imperial decree. The Master [Dahui Zonggao] joyfully submitted to his training. Wuzu was not lenient in his guidance;
the Master earnestly requested instruction, to which Wuzu replied, "If you wish for this matter to reach its true correspondence, you must undergo a death once.

The Master attained a profound realization and recorded it himself in a brief note, the gist of which says: "My house was poor and met with robbery; who would have known that everything had been stripped away?"
[The Master] remained. The room was empty and unoccupied. Several times thieves came and struck it. When Yuanwu saw this, he instructed him to provide extra protection.
In the winter of the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era, the Duke [Wang], along with Grand Secretary Wang Zao, Chancellor Li Bing, and Vice Minister Zeng Kai, went to Mount Jing to visit Dahui.
Upon hearing of their arrival, Dahui ordered the drum to be beaten for them to enter his room. The Duke joyfully approached him, carrying incense in his sleeve.
Dahui asked, "How do you understand the story of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl? The layman said, "What kind of bowl are you looking for? and, shaking his sleeves, he departed.
Dahui rose, grabbed him, and said, "The ancients attained enlightenment right here; why have you not?
As the layman was about to respond, Dahui struck him and said, "What kind of bowl are you looking for? The layman replied, "I am returning..."
This old man has finally attained it.
Xu Fu (who inherited the Dharma from Zhaojue Qin), the State Councilor of the Song Dynasty—
Xu Fu, courtesy name Shichuan, a native of Fenning, styled Donghu Jushi— served as Acting Secretary of the Department of State Affairs during the Jianyan era.
While serving as a Grand Councilor (Shumiyinshi), he frequently attended upon the late Dragon Diagram Master (Longtu) to visit the Chan masters Fachang and Linyuan.

He engaged in discourse with them all day long, yet he regarded their words with indifference. However, when Fachang passed away amidst casual conversation, the official was struck by this and began to believe deeply in this Way.
Later, while observing the mourning period for his father, he felt that nothing could repay his boundless debt of gratitude; he therefore invited Linyuan to come to the site of his filial tomb.
He ascended the seat to preach the Dharma. After the exchange of questions and answers, he said:

"O virtuous ones, as for Longtu, who in his daily life read ten thousand scrolls of books—passing them from vessel to vessel like water, without losing a single drop—tell me, where did he usually keep them?
Now that he has cast off consciousness, where has this one who possessed those ten thousand scrolls gone?"
Upon hearing this, the Duke was suddenly enlightened and said, "I have no further regrets.
Lingyuan descended from his seat and asked, "Scholar, what did you just see that led you to speak in such a manner? The Duke replied, "If there were anything seen, I would have failed the Master.
Lingyuan said, "In that case, I am not your equal. The Duke asked, "Master, what [do you see]?"
"Mind-activity. Lingyuan laughed heartily. At the beginning of the Jingkang era, he served as a *shangshu waibang* (Minister of the Imperial Secretariat).

Together with several fellow officials of like-minded intent, he hung his alms bowl in the Zemo Hall of Tianning Temple and applied himself diligently to the study of Yuanwu. Yuanwu also took delight in his transcendent realization.
One day, [Lingyuan] went to the office of the *shuji* (secretary) and, pointing to Yuanwu’s portrait, said: "The feet of this old fellow..."
[Zhaozhou] was still standing with his feet not touching the ground. Yuanwu turned his face away and said, "How could the turtle ever have escaped from the jar?
Zhaozhou said, "I am glad the old man’s feet are now planted on the ground. Yuanwu said, "Do not slander him. Zhaozhou then withdrew.
Mo Jiang (Sishifa Daisui Jing), Minister of the Board of Rites of the Song Dynasty.

His courtesy name was Shaohu. A native of Yuzhang, he rose to the rank of Minister. While serving in Western Sichuan, he visited Chan Master Nantang Jing to inquire about the essentials for resolving his mind.
Nantang instructed him to maintain mindfulness toward the "good place. Just as he had gone to the latrine, he suddenly smelled a foul odor.

A draft wind blew suddenly; he quickly covered his nose with his hand and attained realization. He immediately presented this verse: "From the beginning, my natural grace has loved elegance; I have often laughed at those who seek it outwardly.
Though there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, there is no place to find it; The moment it is attained, it is right here at the tip of the nose.
Nantang replied: "When a single dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are complete; With its transverse and vertical wondrous function, what more is there to seek?"

The blue serpent emerges from its case and the demonic armies submit; the blue-eyed barbarian smiles and nods his head. (The *Fengxin Song* says: "Having grasped the gold, one needlessly suffers distress;
though it may be elegant, it is but a vain display of style. Had it been used as it is today, it would have severed the stinking nose of the Minister.")
Wang Xiao (Sifa Daisui Jing), a Dragon Diagram Officer of the Song Dynasty, whose courtesy name was Guanfù, held the office of Longtu.
While staying at Zhaojue Temple, he attained realization upon hearing the sound of the board signaling the end of meditation.
He asked Nantang, "I have a certain point of view, yet as soon as someone questions me, I am unable to speak. I wonder where my fault lies.
Nantang replied, "Your fault lies in having a certain point of view. Nantang then asked, "When did you arrive at your post?
The official said, "The fourth day of the eighth month last year. Nantang asked again, "How long has it been since you left the position of Censor-in-Chief?"
In the Yua [prefecture], the Duke said: "On the twentieth of last month, Nantang asked, 'Why is it said that one cannot open one's mouth?
At this, the Duke attained awakening.
This was Song Canzheng Li Bing (who received the Dharma from Jingshan Daoyuan).

Li Bing, courtesy name Hanlao, was a native of Rencheng in Jizhou. He was appointed as a Participant in State Affairs (*Chen-zhi Zheng-shi*). For many years, the official had been devoted to the Way of the Patriarchs (*Zu-dao*).
Upon hearing that Dahui criticized "silent illumination" (*mo-zhao*) as heterodox Chan, he felt a mixture of doubt and indignation.

However, when he saw Dahui address the assembly by citing Zhaozhou’s public case regarding the courtyard cypress, saying: "The cypress tree in the courtyard—today I cite it anew," [he was struck]. He struck [the gong].

"Breaking through Zhaozhou’s Barrier. He sought out words for no other reason. [The Master] asked the assembly, "Since you have already broken through Zhaozhou’s Barrier, why do you still go out of your way to seek words?
After a long silence, he said, "At first I only spoke of the length of the thatch; it was only after burning it that I knew the ground was uneven.
Gōng attained realization and said to Tiānhuì, "Had it not been for the Master’s later words, I would have nearly missed it."

[He] apologized. Later, he sent a letter for consultation, saying: "I recently visited the Hall of Counting Sticks (Kouchushi). I humbly received your inspiration, which cleared away my ignorance and stagnation, and suddenly I attained a realization.

Looking back at myself, I see that my faculties and consciousness are dull and obtuse; all the learning and understanding I have acquired throughout my life have fallen entirely into the realm of emotional views (*qingjian*). With every taking and every rejecting,"
It is like a person wearing tattered rags walking through weeds and thorns, only to become entangled; now, with a single laugh, all my doubts are instantly dispelled.
My joy and gratitude are immeasurable. Were it not for the Great Master’s compassionate and patient guidance, how could this have been achieved?

Since arriving in the city, I have put on my clothes, eaten my meals, and embraced my children and grandchildren—all things remain as they were. Having no feelings of attachment or constraint, I do not even form [artificial] conceptions.

A sense of wonder and marvel arose within me. My other habitual tendencies and long-standing obstacles have also somewhat diminished. I dare not forget the words of exhortation you gave me as I was departing.
Reflecting deeply, I consider that although I have recently gained entry to the gate, the Great Dharma has not yet been clarified;

in responding to circumstances and engaging with others, I am still unable to remain unimpeded in every matter. I further hope for your guidance and instruction so that I may ultimately reach my destination, and thus avoid bringing blemish upon [the lineage].

This concludes the Dharma assembly. Furthermore, he wrote in a letter: "Recently, I have had the honor of receiving your instructions and responses, through which I have fully comprehended the profound meaning. There are three points by which I have personally verified this for myself:

first, regarding matters, whether adverse or favorable, they respond according to conditions without remaining within my breast; second, although my past habitual tendencies are thick and heavy, they naturally diminish without the need for deliberate effort to dispel them;
third, regarding the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients, which I previously found utterly bewildered, I now occasionally experience sudden flashes of insight. This is not..."
Regarding "tasting it for oneself": the aforementioned statement that the Great Dharma was not yet fully clarified was made out of a fear that one might settle for a mere fragment;

it was intended that you expand and fulfill it, rather than seeking some other superior understanding. As for the manifestation of the pure and sublime stream, there is indeed a principle for it; how could I dare not engrave this in my heart?
Liu Yanxiu (posthumously titled Baoxue), who inherited the Dharma from Jingshan Hongzhi, was styled Ziyu.
He held the office of Baoxue and was appointed as the Prefect of Yongjia. There, he went to seek the Way from Chan Master Dahui.
Dahui said: "A monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does even a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou replied, 'No.'"
"Simply look in this way. Later, Gūgong attained enlightenment regarding the cypress tree and composed a verse, saying: "The Zhaozhou Cypress is truly reckless;
To seek it within the realm of objects is also most difficult. Everywhere the green willows can tether a horse;
At every household’s gate, one penetrates Chang’an."
Wu Weiming (Sishifa Jingshan Gao), Provincial Judicial Commissioner of Song.

Wu Weiming, courtesy name Yuanshao, served as a Provincial Judicial Commissioner. He had long attended upon Chan Master Zhenxie Le and attained the Samādhi of Self-Enjoyment as his ultimate realization.
Later, he visited Dahui at the Yangyu Hermitage and entered the room with the assembly. Dahui raised [a koan]:
When asked about the kōan "The Dog Has No Buddha-nature," the Master (Furong Daokai) was about to answer when Dahui struck him with his bamboo staff.
The Master had no reply and remained there to seek instruction. One day, Dahui said to him, "There is no need to display your cleverness;
you must simply 'snap' and 'break through'—only then can you confront birth and death. If you merely display your cleverness, what end will there ever be? Thereupon, the Master took his leave.
On his way, he reached Yanping, where he suddenly attained enlightenment. He immediately composed several verses and sent them to Dahui;
these were all responses to questions posed within the [Dahui] quarters. One said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not an object. My entire body is a set of golden chain-bones."
Zhaozhou personally met the old Nanquan; he understood how to say, "In Zhenzhou they produce radishes. Dahui spoke a verse to certify this, saying:
"A whole body of golden chain-bones, Fit to serve as a model for gods and men.
If you wish to recognize Linji’s little page, He is that very same white-handed thief of yore."
Huang Yanjie of Mensi, Song Dynasty (who received the Dharma from Jingshan Daokai).
Huang Yanjie, courtesy name Jiefu, style name Miaode, had his doubts suddenly severed beneath Dahui’s single shout.
Dahui bestowed his robe upon him. He once raised the story of Shoushan’s bamboo switch, up to the point where Ye Xian stepped forward and snatched it away.
He snapped it in two, threw it down the steps, and asked, "What is this? Shoushan said, "Blind. The official said, "When Miaode reaches this point, he is utterly incapable;
however, I do remember a quatrain I once wrote on wax-plum blossoms: 'If one intends to chew the wax at the branch-tip, its fragrance resembles that of the orchid.
Deep within the heavy snows of the village ahead, do not mistake it for a plum blossom from the mountain ridges.'"
Qian Duanli (Successor to the Dharma, Protector of the State, Yuan), Minister of State of the Song Dynasty.
His courtesy name was Chuhe; his style name was Songchuang. He served as high as Minister of State. He attended upon Chan Master Huguo Yuan, through whom he clarified his own fundamental matter.
Later, he reached the ultimate depths regarding every aspect of the essential principles of the Zen school. In the winter of the Bingshen year of the Chunxi era, Jiantang...
He returned to reside at Pingtian and subsequently maintained a close relationship with him. In the autumn of the Dingyou year, he manifested a slight illness.

When Jiantang Ji was invited to his bedside, the Master sat up in the lotus posture; they conversed and laughed for some time, after which he wrote: "This floating world is illusory; fundamentally, there is no coming or going."
The four elements and five aggregates must ultimately come to an end; they are merely the temporary convergence of earth, water, fire, and wind, and one must not mistakenly identify them as oneself.
Since the sages of antiquity attained freedom in both going and staying, how joyful it is that I am now like this!
Setting down his brush, he looked at Jiandang and said, "It is well to go while sitting; it is well to go while lying down. Jiandang said, "If you, Excellency, go, then [it is well]."
[He said,] "I understand. What need is there to concern myself with sitting or lying down? The Master laughed and said, "Dharma-brother, you must cherish yourself for the sake of the ancestral path.
Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away.
Song Neihan Zeng Kai (who received the Dharma from Lingyin Yuan).
Zeng Kai, style name Tianyou, served as an official up to the rank of Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
He had long studied under Yuanwu and had been visiting Dahui’s gate for many years. In the *Xinwei* year of the Shaoxing era (1171), when Chan Master Fohai Yuan was residing at Sanqu, Mr.
Zeng and the layman Chaoran Zhao went to visit him. They asked, "What is a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)? Fohai replied, "The lantern."
"A pillar. A cat. A dog. The Official said, "Why is it that praise brings joy and disparagement brings affliction?
Fohai said, "Minister, have you ever met a true teacher (Sanskrit: *kalyāṇamitra*)? The Official replied, "I have been seeking instruction for thirty years;
how can you say I have not seen one? Fohai said, "Look where there is joy; look where there is affliction. As the Official hesitated, Fohai gave a shout.
Sheng let out a shout. As the Official prepared to respond, Fohai said, "The one who opens his mouth is not [the truth].

The Official was bewildered. Fohai called out, "Where have you gone, Minister? The Official suddenly attained realization and nodded his head. He then spoke this verse: "Ha! This blind donkey, a pestilence in the monastic groves!
With a single roar that shakes the earth, the celestial mechanism has been leaked. If someone were to ask further about the Way..."
"What? [Zhaozhou] picked up his whisk and struck him across the mouth. Fohai said, "He has only attained one peg. [Zhaozhou] again sent a letter to Dahui, saying:

"Since my youth, I have resolved to seek the Way, visiting and paying respects to spiritual teachers and questioning them about this matter. After reaching the age of twenty, however, I was occupied with marriage and official duties; my practice was not pure, and I have let time pass until now that I am old. I have heard nothing of realization and constantly feel self-reproach and lamentation."

Now, fortunately, my worldly attachments in private life have all come to an end; dwelling in leisure with no affairs, I am currently urging myself on with great earnestness to fulfill my original vow. My only regret is that I have not yet been able to receive your personal instruction and guidance. All the failures and shortcomings of my life have already been presented to you one by one; you will surely be able to clearly perceive this mind of mine.

I hope you will provide me with detailed exhortation and warning as to how I should practice in my daily life, so that I may avoid wandering onto other paths and instead directly accord with the fundamental ground. Though such talk reveals many failings, I am only now casting myself in sincere devotion.

It is truly pitiable that you find it so difficult to conceal or escape from this. Upon receiving your letter, Dàhuì replied: "Since you are a scholar-official, even sages and worthies could not avoid the civil service examinations, marriage, and official career. However, from time to time, amidst moments of stillness and excellence, you must by all means not forget these two phrases:

'Lay down the burden of Mount Sumeru' and 'Let go. Simply proceed from this very point with earnest practice. Do not fear what has already passed, nor need you dwell upon it; for such dwelling in fear and anxiety obstructs the Way."
The Layman Pan Lianggui (d.u.), Court Attendant for the Imperial Secretariat, who succeeded to the Dharma of Fodeng Xun.
His courtesy name was Yirong. A native of Jinhua, he turned his mind toward the ancestral gate at the age of forty.
Wherever he went, he hung his alms bowl and joined the assembly to seek instruction. Later, he relied upon Fodeng, but after a long time, they did not reach a point of accord.
He therefore complained, saying, "Lianggui, I only wish to know: at the moment of death, what will it be like? Fodeng replied, "A fine wrapping; keep it for future use."
Now, failing to understand what is improper, you have suddenly had the outer wrapping changed by another; there is no way to rectify this.
The Master [Zhaozhou] again asked about Nanquan’s story of killing the cat, saying, "I have contemplated this for a very long time, yet I still have not fully penetrated it.
I pray the Venerable will show me compassion. Fodeng said, "You are merely occupied with trying to understand someone else's cat; you do not realize that your own has run away."
"Your own dog. Under these words, Gong was as if awakened from a drunken stupor.

Minister Li Hao (who received the Dharma from Tiantong Hua), Minister Li Hao, styled De-yuan and nicknamed Zheng-xin, read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in his youth and felt as though he were returning to a familiar home.
He remained resolute and never forgot [the teachings]. Serving as a scribe (*tuo*) behind [the master], he eventually visited Mingguo, where he entered the inner chamber with sincere devotion.
Ying’an tested his resolve, asking: "After the Minister dies, where will you go? The official was struck with terror and broke into a sweat. Ying’an shouted at him and sent him out.
He withdrew to practice meditation, and within ten days, he finally ascended to the inner sanctum. He sent a verse to his fellow practitioner Yan Kangchao, which began: "At the gate is a grandson..."

At Binpu, the wife of Gan Zhi resided. Sleeping at night and rising early in the morning—who awakens and who is deluded? Ying’an praised her as virtuous. There was also a seller of rouge who had likewise studied under Ying’an for a long time and prided herself greatly.

The Master bestowed upon her this verse: Binpu’s house harbors the wife of Gan Zhi; Sleeping at night and rising before dawn— Who realizes it, and who remains lost? Ying’an recognized her excellence. There was also a seller of rouge who had long attended Ying’an and was quite conceited. The Master gave her this verse:
Without applying rouge or powder, he is naturally elegant; often it is here that practitioners of Zen come to their rest.
Having passed through the snares of past and present, they return here to receive a blow of the fist.

The Thirteenth Monk Wu of Song (who inherited the Dharma from Kaishan Qian) was at Mount Xianzhou in Jianning Prefecture. The Thirteenth Monk Wu constantly used his own practice to question various Chan masters.

When Kaishan returned, he built a thatched hut to the left of the mountain, and the monk subsequently went there to serve him. On the eighth day of the third month in the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era, at night—
Suddenly, he attained enlightenment. He composed a verse and presented it to Kaishan, saying: "Originally there has been no seam or crack; Upon being touched, it immediately radiates light.
Since it is a treasure worth a thousand pieces of gold, Why need one use a pellet to shoot at a sparrow? Kaishan replied: "When it snaps with a *chui* sound, true joy and ease arise;
Birth-and-death, ordinary and sage—all sink into stillness. Laughing "he-he" beneath Mount Xianzhou, I have not betrayed our long-standing mutual expectation."
*The Ancient Mind:
A Commentary on the Lineage of the First Patriarchs*, Volume Three, by Shuangji Shutunrang.
Subscription for *The Lineage of the First Patriarchs*, Volume Four.
Edited by the Elder Fenyang of Mount Jing, Yuanxin;
verified by the Master of No Ground, Guo Ningzhi;
compiled by Yang Xuanzhi.

Yang Xuanzhi of the Northern Wei served as the Governor of Qicheng. From an early age, he had admired the Buddha-vehicle. When Bodhidharma arrived in the Wei, he resided at Qiansheng Temple on Mount Yumen.
Yang Xuanzhi asked him, saying: "I, your disciple, have turned my heart toward the Triple Gem for many years;
yet my wisdom remains clouded and obscure, and I am still lost regarding the True Principle. I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will reveal the essential tenets. Bodhidharma spoke this verse:
One does not harbor aversion upon seeing evil, nor exert oneself in the practice of good. One does not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly, nor cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment.
To reach the Great Way is to transcend all measure; to penetrate the Buddha-mind is to go beyond all limits.
Not sharing the same orbit as ordinary beings or sages, he was transcendentally named a Patriarch. Xuanzhi, filled with a mixture of grief and joy, said:
"I only pray that you will dwell long in this world to transform and guide all living beings."
Song Yun, Song Yun—envoys of the Northern Wei dynasty—were dispatched by Empress Dowager Hu to travel to the Western Regions alongside the bhikṣu Hui-sheng to seek Buddhist scriptures.
After traveling four thousand li, they reached Mount Qi (Chiling), where they finally emerged from the borders of the Wei realm. Continuing westward for another two years, they arrived at Qianluo.
Faguang returned from the country with one hundred and seventy volumes of Buddhist scriptures. Upon crossing Xi Ling, he saw Bodhidharma’s single sandal fluttering away as it departed alone.
Faguang asked, "Where is the Master going? He replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven. Faguang returned and recounted the matter in detail.
At that time, Bodhidharma had already been deceased; when his disciples opened his tomb, there was nothing there but a single sandal.
Addressed to the Layman:

You dwell in seclusion within the forests and wilds, eating from the trees and drinking from the mountain streams. At the beginning of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi dynasty, having heard of the flourishing transformation wrought by the Second Patriarch, he sent him a letter saying:
"Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To toy with shadows is to weary the form; thus one fails to recognize the form itself."
It serves as the original for its reflection. To raise one's voice and seek to stop the echo is not to realize that sound is the root of the echo.

To eliminate afflictions while rushing toward Nirvana is like discarding the form to search for the shadow; it is like departing from sentient beings to seek the fruit of Buddhahood; it is like remaining silent to seek an echo.

Therefore, know that delusion and awakening are of one path, and the ignorant and the wise are not distinct. Where there is no name, names are created; because names are employed, right and wrong arise.
To take what is irrational as rational, one follows that logic and disputes arise. Illusions are not real; who is right and who is wrong?
They are empty fabrications without substance; what is void and what exists? One should know that in gain there is nothing gained, and in loss there is nothing lost.

Before I have had the opportunity to pay my respects in person, I have briefly set forth this meaning. I humbly hope for a reply. The Second Patriarch replied: "I have carefully observed the purport of your letter."
All are as they truly are; the principle of ultimate profundity is ultimately no different. Originally deluded, one mistook the mani-jewel for rubble;
suddenly awakening, one realizes it is a genuine pearl. Ignorance and wisdom are equal and without distinction; one should know that all phenomena are thus.
Out of compassion for those who hold these two views, I have composed this book with pen and word. Behold that the body and the Buddha are not distinct—how [could there be any difference]?

"One must further seek an opportunity; there is no other way. The layman (Jushi) then respectfully received and recited the Patriarch’s verse, whereupon he prostrated himself in audience and secretly received the seal of transmission (*mudrā*).

Du Hongjian, whose courtesy name was Zixun, was a native of Puyang in Puzhou. His family had followed the Buddhist faith for generations; he served as the chief strategist for Lingwu.
A meritorious official, he later served as Chancellor and pacified Yizhou. He dispatched an envoy to Mount Baitia to invite Chan Master Wuzhu into the city to inquire about the Dharma.
The official said, "I have heard from the Master that you preach the three-phrased Dharma-gate of 'no-recollection,' 'no-thought,' and 'no-delusion.
I do not yet know whether these are one or three. Wuzhu replied, "No-recollection is called Precept; no-thought is called Concentration; no-delusion is called Wisdom."
"Delusion" (*wang*) is named after wisdom (*hui*). When the single mind does not arise, one is already endowed with precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither one nor three. The Duke asked:

"In the latter phrase, is the character 'delusion' (*wang*) the same as the 'forgetting' (*wang*) that is written with the 'heart' radical? He replied: "The one written with the 'woman' radical is correct.

The Duke asked: "Is there scriptural authority for this? He replied: "The *Dharmapada-sūtra* says: 'If one gives rise to a mind of striving, this is delusion, not true diligence. If one can ensure the mind is not deluded...'"
"His diligence knows no bounds. The Duke asked again, "Does the Master still teach people by means of the three phrases?
Wuzhu replied, "For a beginner practitioner, one first causes them to cease their thoughts and settle the waves of consciousness. When the water is clear, the reflection appears;

having realized the essence of non-thought, quiescent extinction manifests before them, and even 'non-thought' is no longer established. At that moment, a crow cawed in a tree in the courtyard. Wuzhu asked, "Lord, did you hear that?"
"Were you hearing? he asked. "I was," he replied. After the crow had left, he asked again, "Are you hearing now? He replied, "The crow has gone and there is no sound; how can one say one is hearing?
Wuzhu said, "Hearing and not hearing do not concern the nature of hearing. When there is sound, it is merely the auditory object (śabda-dhātu) that arises of itself."
When there is no sound, it is the object of sound that ceases of its own accord; yet this nature of hearing does not arise with the sound, nor does it cease with the sound.
To realize this nature of hearing is to escape the cycle of transmigration caused by the objects of sound. This applies equally to forms, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.
The Duke was filled with joy and exclaimed, "Excellent! He asked again, "What is called the 'Ultimate Truth' (paramārtha)? The Ultimate Truth is— [from]...

"How does one enter [the path] in sequence? Wuzhu said, "The ultimate truth (paramārtha) has no sequence; it neither enters nor exits. In conventional truth (saṃvṛti), everything exists; in the ultimate truth, there is nothing.

The Master said, "That which has existence is called conventional truth; that which lacks intrinsic nature is the ultimate truth. Wuzhu said, "As you, Master, have explained, this is truly not possible."
[The Master] said, "It is inconceivable. The Master further said, "Your disciple’s nature and understanding are shallow.
Previously, during my leisure time, I composed two fascicles of commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*. May these be called the Buddha-dharma? Wuzhu replied, "All dharmas, from the very beginning,"

It is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects. It is ultimately equal and without change;

it is simply the one mind, and is therefore called True Suchness (*tathatā*). Now, you, Excellency, are attached to the characteristic of verbal expression, attached to the characteristic of names and words, and attached to the characteristic of mental objects.
Since you are attached to these various characteristics, how can this be the Buddha-dharma? You asked again: "What is non-arising?"
"How is it that there is no extinction? How does one attain liberation? Wuzhu said: "When the mind does not arise upon encountering objects, this is called non-arising.
Non-arising is itself non-extinction. Since there is neither arising nor extinction, one is not bound by external sensory realms; one is liberated in that very place."
Non-arising is called non-thought. Non-thought is itself non-extinction. Non-thought is itself non-bondage. Non-thought is itself non-liberation. To state the essential point:
when the mind of consciousness ceases, one is free from thought; when the nature is seen, one is liberated. Apart from ceasing the mind of consciousness and seeing the nature, there is nothing else.
"Furthermore, there is no possibility of attaining unsurpassed bodhi through any other dharma-gate. Gong asked, "What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing the nature'?

This essence of the mind is ultimately unattainable; there is nothing to be known or perceived. Everything one encounters is thus; there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the nature of seeing. Master Gong.

The Chan Master said: "One who has realized the principle and stilled delusion does not form karma. After the end of this single lifetime, upon what does their numinous spirit rely?
Guifeng said: "All sentient beings are without exception endowed with the nature of awakening. Its numinous clarity and empty stillness are no different from that of a Buddha.
It is only because, since beginningless kalpas, they have never attained realization, and thus falsely cling to the body as the mark of self, that [this occurs]."

One gives rise to emotions such as love and hatred; following these emotions, one creates karma; following that karma, one undergoes retribution. Thus, through birth, old age, sickness, and death, one transmigrates in saṃsāra for long kalpas.
Yet the enlightened nature within the body has never experienced birth or death; it is like being driven and enslaved in a dream, while the body remains fundamentally at ease.
It is like water forming ice, yet its moist nature does not change. If one can awaken to this nature, it is itself the Dharmakāya.
Being originally unborn, how could there be any dependence? It is luminous and never obscured; it is clear and ever-knowing. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Yet, through many lifetimes of deluded attachments, these have become habitual and formed into a nature; the subtle flow of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure is difficult to perceive.
Eliminate them completely. One must constantly maintain vigilance. Regard emptiness and stillness as one's own essence; do not identify with the physical body.
Regard luminous awareness as one's own mind; do not identify with deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. At the time of death—
Karma produced by nature cannot bind them. Although they possess the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), their destination is free;
they may dwell at will among devas or humans. Once the thoughts of love and hatred have vanished, they no longer receive a body of segmented birth.
The great wisdom of perfect enlightenment remains alone, radiant and clear—this is what is called "Buddha. Guifeng previously had an eight-line verse that elucidates this meaning. The verse says:
To perform deeds that accord with the meaningful is the awakened mind; to perform deeds that accord with the meaningless is the deluded mind.

The deluded mind follows emotional impulses, and at the moment of death, one is dragged away by karma. The awakened mind does not follow emotional impulses, and at the moment of death, it can transform karma.

The Man from Shishan—his personal name is lost to history—posed ten questions to Chan Master Guifeng. First Question: What is the Way?
How is it cultivated? Must it necessarily be accomplished through cultivation, or does it not require effort? Answer: It is unimpeded.

This is the Way. Awakening to delusion is cultivation. Although the Way is fundamentally perfect, the arising of delusion acts as a hindrance. When delusive thoughts are completely exhausted, cultivation is perfected. Second Question: If the Way is accomplished through cultivation, it would be a product of conditioned effort and thus identical to worldly dharmas—false, unreal, and subject to destruction after its formation. How can it be called "transcending the world"? Answer: Conditioned effort constitutes karmic bondage and is termed "false. The Way is not produced by effort; it is inherently present. It is only because of delusion that one fails to realize it. Therefore, awakening to delusion is called cultivation. Once delusion is exhausted, the Way is spontaneously realized. This is why it is called "transcending the world. It is not something newly created. Thus, there is no contradiction with the principle of non-arising. Furthermore, the nature of the mind is originally pure; it is only due to adventitious delusions that it appears defiled. If one awakens to this and exhausts all delusions, the original purity is restored. This is precisely what is meant by "transcending the world. It is not a dharma produced by effort. Therefore, it is not false or unreal. Since it is not produced by effort, it does not undergo destruction. Hence, it is called "eternal" and "unchanging. It is not like worldly dharmas, which are produced by effort and therefore perish. Because the Way is not produced by effort, it is not subject to destruction. This is why it is called "transcending the world. It is not a dharma of the three realms. Because it transcends the three realms, it is called "supramundane. Because it is supramundane, it is called "nirvana. Because it is nirvana, it is called "Buddhahood. Because it is Buddhahood, it is called "the Great Vehicle. Because it is the Great Vehicle, it is called "the Ultimate Truth. Because it is the Ultimate Truth, it is called "the One Vehicle. Because it is the One Vehicle, it is called "the Unsurpassed. Because it is unsurpassed, it is called "the Peerless. Because it is peerless, it is called "the Sovereign. Because it is sovereign, it is called "the All-Pervading. Because it is all-pervading, it is called "the Source of All Dharmas. Because it is the source of all dharmas, it is called "the Mother of Buddhas. Because it is the mother of Buddhas, it is called "the Treasury of Jewels. Because it is the treasury of jewels, it is called "the Dharma Body. Because it is the Dharma Body, it is called "the Tathāgata. Because it is the Tathāgata, it is called "the World-Honored One. Because it is the World-Honored One, it is called "the Buddha. Because it is the Buddha, it is called "the Awakened One. Because it is the Awakened One, it is called "the Enlightened One. Question Six: Form is not form. All sutras state that one delivers sentient beings. Yet, sentient beings are themselves non-sentient beings.
Why then do you laboriously deliver them? Answer: If sentient beings were real, delivering them would indeed be laborious.

Since you yourself say they are "non-sentient beings," why not apply the same logic to their delivery such that there is no delivery at all? Question Seven: Various sutras state that the Buddha is eternally abiding, or...
It is said that the Buddha enters extinction; yet if he were eternal, he would not be extinguished, and if he were extinguished, he would not be eternal—how could these not be contradictory?
Answer: To be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas. How could there be any reality to his appearing in the world or entering extinction?

Those who perceive his appearance and disappearance do so according to the conditions of sentient beings (*karmic capacity*). When the conditions respond, he appears beneath the Bodhi tree; when the conditions are exhausted, he [enters] the *śāla* grove.
Entering *nirvāṇa* amidst the forest, it is like pure water that is without mind: no image appears, yet the image is not "mine. This is merely the coming and going of external forms;

Question: Birth is the cessation of mind; phenomena are the cessation of birth. How, then, does one attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)? Answer:

Since it is said that all things are like transformations, and transformations are emptiness, and emptiness is non-arising, why inquire about the meaning of arising? Once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is the truth.

To accept and confirm this dharma of non-arising is called the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena. Ninth Question: The Buddhas’ attainment of the Way and their preaching of the Dharma are solely for the sake of—

"Not so. Huijue said, "What about that which cannot be grasped? Song was unable to respond. Wang Shenzhi (王審知), courtesy name Xintong (信通), was a native of Guangzhou.
